name: Collection Framework

beginner.content:
What is Collection Framework?

A Collection Framework is a unified architecture that provides a set of classes and interfaces to store, manipulate, and retrieve groups of objects efficiently. In simple terms: Framework = Classes + Interfaces.

Why Do We Need Collections?

In Java, arrays have several limitations:

  • Fixed Size - Once an array is created, its size cannot be changed. You must know the size in advance, which can lead to wasted memory or insufficient space.
  • Homogeneous - Arrays can only store elements of the same data type. You cannot mix different types in a single array.
  • No Readymade Methods - Arrays do not provide built-in methods for common operations like sorting, searching, or removing elements.

Differences Between Array and Collection


  • Size: Arrays are fixed size; Collections are growable (dynamic size).
  • Data Types: Arrays are homogeneous; Collections can hold heterogeneous objects.
  • Methods: Arrays have no readymade methods; Collections provide readymade methods (add, remove, contains, sort, etc.).
  • Primitives: Arrays can hold primitives; Collections can only hold objects (use wrapper classes for primitives).
  • Memory: Arrays may waste memory; Collections manage memory dynamically.

Collection Hierarchy

The Collection Framework has a well-defined hierarchy:

  • Iterable(I) - Root interface
  • Collection(I) - Extends Iterable
    • List(I) - Ordered, allows duplicates (ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, Stack)
    • Set(I) - Unordered, no duplicates (HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet)
    • Queue(I) - FIFO ordering (PriorityQueue, Deque)

  • Map(I) - Separate hierarchy, key-value pairs (HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, Hashtable)

The 9 Key Interfaces of the Collection Framework

The framework is built around 9 core interfaces: Collection, List, Set, SortedSet, NavigableSet, Queue, Map, SortedMap, and NavigableMap.

  • Collection is considered the root interface of the framework - it defines the most common methods applicable to any collection object (add, remove, size, etc.).
  • There is no concrete class that implements the Collection interface directly - you always work through one of its child interfaces (List, Set, Queue) and their implementing classes.

Collection Framework Hierarchy at a Glance

A clean side-by-side view of every interface, its key implementing classes, and its defining behavior:

InterfaceExtendsImplementing ClassesOrderDuplicates
ListCollectionArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, StackInsertion orderAllowed
SetCollectionHashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSetNo / insertion / sortedNot allowed
QueueCollectionPriorityQueue, ArrayDeque, LinkedListFIFO (or priority)Allowed
DequeQueueArrayDeque, LinkedListBoth endsAllowed
Map(none - separate hierarchy)HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, HashtableDepends on impl.Keys unique, values may repeat

Note: Map is deliberately NOT part of the Collection interface hierarchy - it stores key-value pairs rather than single elements, so its method contract (put/get by key) is fundamentally different from add/remove used by List, Set, and Queue.

Iterable and Collection Interfaces

The Iterable interface is the root of the collection hierarchy. Any class that implements Iterable can be used with the enhanced for-each loop. It provides the iterator() method.

Collection Interface Methods

The Collection interface extends Iterable and defines the most common operations for all collections:

  • add(Object o) - Adds an element to the collection
  • addAll(Collection c) - Adds all elements from another collection
  • remove(Object o) - Removes a single instance of the specified element
  • removeAll(Collection c) - Removes all elements that are in the specified collection
  • retainAll(Collection c) - Retains only elements that are in the specified collection
  • clear() - Removes all elements from the collection
  • contains(Object o) - Returns true if the collection contains the element
  • containsAll(Collection c) - Returns true if the collection contains all elements of the specified collection
  • isEmpty() - Returns true if the collection is empty
  • size() - Returns the number of elements
  • toArray() - Converts the collection to an array
  • iterator() - Returns an Iterator over the elements

List Interface Specifics

The List interface extends Collection and represents an ordered collection (sequence). Key characteristics:

  • Ordered - Elements maintain their insertion order
  • Allows Duplicates - Same element can appear multiple times
  • Index-Based Access - Elements can be accessed by their integer index

Additional List Methods

  • get(int index) - Returns element at specified index
  • set(int index, Object o) - Replaces element at specified index
  • indexOf(Object o) - Returns first occurrence index, or -1
  • lastIndexOf(Object o) - Returns last occurrence index, or -1
  • listIterator() - Returns a ListIterator for bidirectional traversal
  • subList(int from, int to) - Returns a view of the portion between from (inclusive) and to (exclusive)

Queue and Deque Interfaces

The Queue interface extends Collection and represents a collection designed for holding elements prior to processing, typically in FIFO (First-In-First-Out) order.

Key Queue Methods (Pairs That Behave Differently on Failure)


OperationThrows ExceptionReturns Special Value
Insertadd(e)offer(e)
Removeremove()poll()
Examineelement()peek()

Deque (Double-Ended Queue)

Deque extends Queue and allows insertion/removal from both ends - front and rear. It can be used as both a Queue (FIFO) and a Stack (LIFO). ArrayDeque is the recommended, faster, non-synchronized replacement for the legacy Stack class.

  • addFirst(e) / addLast(e) - Insert at front / rear
  • removeFirst() / removeLast() - Remove from front / rear
  • peekFirst() / peekLast() - Examine front / rear without removing
  • push(e) / pop() - Stack-style operations (both act on the front)
codeExamples:
import java.util.*;  // imports every class of java.util

public class DequeDemo {                            // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {        // program entry point
        Deque<Integer> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();  // creates an empty ArrayDeque named deque

        // Insert at both ends
        deque.addFirst(10);                     // adds 10 at the front
        deque.addLast(20);                      // adds 20 at the end
        deque.addFirst(5);                      // adds 5 at the front
        deque.addLast(25);                      // adds 25 at the end
        System.out.println("Deque: " + deque);  // [5, 10, 20, 25]

        // Use as a Stack (LIFO) - push/pop act on the front
        deque.push(1);                                  // pushes 1 on top of the stack
        System.out.println("After push(1): " + deque);  // [1, 5, 10, 20, 25]
        System.out.println("pop(): " + deque.pop());    // 1

        // Use as a Queue (FIFO)
        System.out.println("pollFirst(): " + deque.pollFirst());  // 5
        System.out.println("pollLast(): " + deque.pollLast());  // 25
        System.out.println("Final Deque: " + deque);            // [10, 20]
    }
}

Iterator vs ListIterator

Java provides different cursor types for traversing collections. Understanding their differences is critical for advanced usage.

Iterator

  • Can traverse any Collection (List, Set, Queue)
  • Supports only forward direction traversal
  • Methods: hasNext(), next(), remove()
  • Obtained via collection.iterator()

ListIterator

  • Can only traverse List objects
  • Supports bidirectional traversal (forward and backward)
  • Methods: hasNext(), next(), hasPrevious(), previous(), nextIndex(), previousIndex(), remove(), set(), add()
  • Obtained via list.listIterator()

Cursor Types in Java


  • Enumeration - Legacy cursor for Vector. Methods: hasMoreElements(), nextElement(). Read-only, forward-only.
  • Iterator - Universal cursor for any Collection. Forward-only. Supports remove operation.
  • ListIterator - Most powerful cursor but only for Lists. Bidirectional. Supports add, set, and remove.

Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterators


  • Fail-Fast Iterators: Immediately throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is structurally modified after the iterator is created (except through the iterator's own methods). Examples: iterators of ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet. They work on the original collection.
  • Fail-Safe Iterators: Do NOT throw ConcurrentModificationException. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates a frozen snapshot taken when the iterator was created, so later changes are invisible to it. ConcurrentHashMap is different: its iterators are weakly consistent - they traverse the live table and MAY reflect updates made after creation, they simply never throw.
codeExamples:
import java.util.*;  // imports every class of java.util

public class IteratorVsListIterator {           // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {    // program entry point
        List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();  // creates an empty ArrayList named list
        list.add("A");                          // adds "A" to the end of the list
        list.add("B");                          // adds "B" to the end of the list
        list.add("C");                          // adds "C" to the end of the list
        list.add("D");                          // adds "D" to the end of the list

        // Iterator - forward only
        System.out.println("--- Iterator (Forward Only) ---");  // prints the text "--- Iterator (Forward Only)..."
        Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();                  // stores the result: gets an iterator to walk the elements
        while (it.hasNext()) {                                  // runs while the iterator has more elements
            System.out.println(it.next());                      // prints the next element
        }

        // ListIterator - bidirectional
        System.out.println("--- ListIterator (Forward) ---");  // prints the text "--- ListIterator (Forward)..."
        ListIterator<String> lit = list.listIterator();        // stores the result: gets a list iterator that can move in both directions
        while (lit.hasNext()) {                                // runs while the iterator has more elements
            System.out.println("Index " + lit.nextIndex() + ": " + lit.next());  // prints the next element
        }

        System.out.println("--- ListIterator (Backward) ---");  // prints the text "--- ListIterator (Backward)..."
        while (lit.hasPrevious()) {                             // runs while there is an earlier element
            System.out.println("Index " + lit.previousIndex() + ": " + lit.previous());  // prints the next element
        }

        // ListIterator - add and set
        lit = list.listIterator();                           // assigns a new value to lit
        while (lit.hasNext()) {                              // runs while the iterator has more elements
            String val = lit.next();                         // stores the result: moves to and returns the next element
            if (val.equals("B")) {                           // checks the condition
                lit.set("B-Modified");                       // replace current
                lit.add("B2-Inserted");                      // insert after current
            }
        }
        System.out.println("After modifications: " + list);  // prints a label followed by the value

        // Fail-Fast example
        try {                                          // code that may throw an exception
            Iterator<String> it2 = list.iterator();    // stores the result: gets an iterator to walk the elements
            list.add("E");                             // structural modification
            it2.next();                                // throws ConcurrentModificationException
        } catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {  // handles ConcurrentModificationException
            System.out.println("Fail-Fast: ConcurrentModificationException caught!");  // prints the text "Fail-Fast: ConcurrentModifi..."
        }
    }
}

Collection Interface vs Collections Utility Class

One of the most common points of confusion for beginners: Collection (singular, an interface) and Collections (plural, a final utility class) are two completely different things that just happen to share a similar name.

Collection (interface)Collections (class)
Root interface of the frameworkfinal utility class in java.util
Defines instance methods like add(), remove()Provides only static helper methods
Implemented by ArrayList, HashSet, etc.Operates ON a collection passed as an argument
Represents an actual group of objectsCannot be instantiated (private constructor)

Commonly Used Collections Utility Methods


  • Collections.sort(list) - Sorts in natural order (or with a Comparator)
  • Collections.reverse(list) - Reverses the order of elements
  • Collections.shuffle(list) - Randomly shuffles elements
  • Collections.max(coll) / Collections.min(coll) - Finds the largest/smallest element
  • Collections.unmodifiableList(list) - Returns a read-only view of the list
  • Collections.synchronizedList(list) - Returns a thread-safe wrapper
  • Collections.emptyList() / emptySet() / emptyMap() - Returns an immutable empty collection
  • Collections.frequency(coll, obj) - Counts how many times an element occurs
codeExamples:
import java.util.*;  // imports every class of java.util

public class CollectionsUtilityDemo {         // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {  // program entry point
        List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 3));  // creates an ArrayList filled with the listed values

        System.out.println("Original: " + numbers);  // prints a label followed by the value

        Collections.sort(numbers);                 // sorts the list (natural order or the given comparator)
        System.out.println("Sorted: " + numbers);  // prints a label followed by the value

        Collections.reverse(numbers);                // reverses the order of the elements
        System.out.println("Reversed: " + numbers);  // prints a label followed by the value

        System.out.println("Max: " + Collections.max(numbers));  // prints a label followed by the value
        System.out.println("Min: " + Collections.min(numbers));  // prints a label followed by the value
        System.out.println("Frequency of 3: " + Collections.frequency(numbers, 3));  // prints a label followed by the value

        // Immutable/read-only view
        List<Integer> readOnly = Collections.unmodifiableList(numbers);  // stores the value in readOnly
        try {                                        // code that may throw an exception
            readOnly.add(100);                       // throws UnsupportedOperationException
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {  // handles UnsupportedOperationException
            System.out.println("Cannot modify unmodifiableList!");  // prints the text "Cannot modify unmodifiableL..."
        }

        // Thread-safe wrapper
        List<Integer> safeList = Collections.synchronizedList(numbers);  // stores the value in safeList
        System.out.println("Synchronized wrapper size: " + safeList.size());  // prints the number of elements
    }
}

Choosing the Right Collection

A quick decision guide for picking the correct collection type based on the requirement:

RequirementBest ChoiceWhy
Fast random access by indexArrayListBacked by array, O(1) get()
Frequent insert/delete in the middleLinkedListO(1) relink once you hold the node - but add(int,E)/remove(int) must traverse first, so the whole operation is O(n)
Thread-safe listVector or Collections.synchronizedList()Synchronized access
LIFO stack behaviorArrayDeque (preferred over Stack)Faster, not synchronized, purpose-built
No duplicates, order doesn't matterHashSetO(1) add/contains
No duplicates, preserve insertion orderLinkedHashSetHash table + linked list
No duplicates, need sorted orderTreeSetRed-Black tree, always sorted
Key-value lookup, order doesn't matterHashMapO(1) average get/put
Key-value lookup, sorted by keyTreeMapRed-Black tree, sorted keys
FIFO processing / task queueArrayDeque or LinkedListImplements Queue naturally
Process by priority, not insertion orderPriorityQueueMin-heap, orders by natural/Comparator order
Thread-safe Map for concurrent accessConcurrentHashMapSegment-level locking, high concurrency

Fresher Notes

  • The Collections Framework is a set of interfaces and classes in java.util for storing and processing groups of objects.
  • Main interfaces: List (ordered, duplicates), Set (unique), Queue/Deque, and Map (key-value, not a Collection).
  • Code to the interface: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();.

Worked Example 1

Fail-fast demo.

Worked Example 2

Unmodifiable view vs copy.
codeExamples:
List<String> src = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));       // creates an ArrayList filled with the listed values
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src);  // stores the value in view
List<String> copy = List.copyOf(src);                   // copy is an immutable list of the listed values
src.add("b");                                           // adds "b" to the end of the list
System.out.println(view + " " + copy);                  // prints the result

// OUTPUT:
// [a, b] [a]

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The framework has two roots: Collection (List, Set, Queue) and Map. Abstract skeletons (AbstractList, AbstractMap) provide partial implementations. Iterable lets any collection work in the for-each loop. Since Java 21, SequencedCollection adds first, last and reversed views to ordered types.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choose by access pattern. Streams give a declarative pipeline over collections: filter, map, collect, groupingBy. Factory methods List.of, Set.of and Map.of return immutable collections that reject nulls. Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view over an array.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Pick by need: ArrayList for fast index access, LinkedList for queue/deque use, HashSet for uniqueness, TreeSet/TreeMap for sorted data, HashMap for lookups.
  • The Collections utility class gives sort, reverse, shuffle, unmodifiableList and synchronizedList.
  • Use List.of, Set.of, Map.of for small immutable collections (Java 9+).

Senior Notes

  • Know complexity: ArrayList get O(1), add amortized O(1); HashMap get O(1) average; TreeMap O(log n).
  • Fail-fast iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException when a collection is changed during iteration; concurrent collections are weakly consistent.
  • Prefer immutable collections and defensive copies at API boundaries; use concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) for threads.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: modifying a collection while iterating, using mutable objects as keys, using raw types, relying on HashSet or HashMap order, using Vector or Hashtable in new code, and returning internal mutable collections from getters (breaks encapsulation). Return copies or unmodifiable views.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance depends on choice: ArrayList iteration is cache friendly, HashMap with a good hash is O(1), and boxing costs memory (an Integer list uses much more than int[]). For primitives consider arrays, IntStream or libraries like fastutil or Eclipse Collections. Measure with JMH before optimizing.
codeExamples:
int n = 5_000_000;                         // declares int n with value 5_000_000
long t0 = System.nanoTime();               // declares long t0 with value System.nanoTime()
List<Integer> boxed = new ArrayList<>(n);  // creates an ArrayList named boxed copied from n
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {              // counting loop
    boxed.add(i);                          // adds i to the end of the list
}
long t1 = System.nanoTime();               // declares long t1 with value System.nanoTime()
int[] prim = new int[n];                   // creates an array named prim
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {              // counting loop
    prim[i] = i;                           // stores i at index i of prim
}
long t2 = System.nanoTime();               // declares long t2 with value System.nanoTime()
System.out.println("boxed ms=" + (t1 - t0) / 1_000_000 + " primitive ms=" + (t2 - t1) / 1_000_000);  // prints a label followed by the value

// OUTPUT: (varies)
// boxed ms=95 primitive ms=6

beginner.content:
What is an ArrayList?

An ArrayList is a resizable array. A normal Java array has a fixed size that you choose once; an ArrayList starts small and grows by itself when you add more elements, and shrinks when you remove them. Think of a list of forts you want to visit: you can add a new fort at the end, insert one in the middle, or cross one off, without ever deciding the size in advance.

  • It lives in the java.util package and implements the List interface (so it is an ordered collection).
  • Order is kept: elements stay in the order you added them, and every element has an index starting at 0.
  • Duplicates are allowed: the same value can appear many times.
  • null is allowed: you can store null (but avoid it in real programs).
  • Fast reading: get(index) is instant, because inside it is an array.
  • Not thread-safe: if several threads change one ArrayList at the same time, wrap it or use a concurrent list (see the Expert tab).
  • It stores objects only. For numbers use the wrapper types: ArrayList<Integer>, not ArrayList<int>.

Where ArrayList sits in the Collection Framework

(I) = interface, (c) = class. ArrayList also implements RandomAccess (a marker that says "index access is fast"), Cloneable and Serializable. In Java 21 List also extends SequencedCollection, which added getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), addLast(), removeFirst(), removeLast() and reversed().

Creating an ArrayList: the three constructors

  • new ArrayList<>(): an empty list. Internally it starts with no array at all and allocates room for 10 elements on the first add.
  • new ArrayList<>(int initialCapacity): an empty list that already has room for that many elements. Use it when you know roughly how many items are coming; it avoids repeated growing.
  • new ArrayList<>(Collection c): a copy of another collection, in that collection's iteration order.

Tip: declare the variable with the interface type, List<String> forts = new ArrayList<>();. Your code then does not care which list class is behind it, and you can switch to another implementation later by changing one word.

Your first ArrayList program

  • add(x) puts x at the end; get(i) reads the element at index i; size() tells how many elements there are.
  • Printing the list shows all elements in [a, b, c] form because ArrayList overrides toString().
  • The last valid index is always size() - 1. Reading beyond it throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

ArrayList stores objects: using numbers

  • Generic type arguments must be classes, so use the wrapper classes Integer, Double, Long, Boolean, Character.
  • Java converts automatically between int and Integer (autoboxing when adding, unboxing when reading).

intermediate.content:
Adding elements

Four ways to put elements in: at the end, at a position, a whole collection at the end, and a whole collection at a position.

add(E e)

  • Signature: boolean add(E e)
  • Returns: true (always, for ArrayList)
  • Time: O(1) amortised

For freshers: Puts the element at the end of the list. The list grows by one. You do not have to check the size first.

For experienced developers: Normally just writes into the next free slot of the internal array. When the array is full it allocates a bigger one (about 1.5 times) and copies, which is why the cost is called amortised O(1): rare expensive growths are spread over many cheap adds. Every structural change also increases modCount, which makes running iterators fail fast.

add(int index, E e)

  • Signature: void add(int index, E element)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n): later elements shift right

For freshers: Inserts the element at the position you choose. The element that was there, and everything after it, moves one step to the right. Valid indexes are 0 to size() (adding at size() is the same as adding at the end).

For experienced developers: Uses System.arraycopy to shift the tail, so inserting near the front of a big list is expensive. If you insert at the front very often, an ArrayDeque or LinkedList may suit better.

Watch out: Index size() + 1 or more throws IndexOutOfBoundsException; you cannot leave gaps in a list.

addAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean addAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the list changed
  • Time: O(m), m = size of c

For freshers: Adds every element of another collection (a list, a set, even a queue) to the end, in that collection's order. It returns false only when you add an empty collection.

For experienced developers: Converts the argument to an array once and copies it in a single block, so it is much faster than calling add in a loop. The argument may hold subtypes of the element type (? extends E).

addAll(int index, Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean addAll(int index, Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the list changed
  • Time: O(n + m)

For freshers: Inserts a whole collection in the middle: the new elements go in at index (in their own order) and the old elements after it shift to the right.

For experienced developers: One shift of the tail plus one copy of the new block. Prefer it over a loop of add(i, e) calls, which would shift the tail once per element.

addFirst(E) and addLast(E) (Java 21)

  • Signature: void addFirst(E e); void addLast(E e)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: addFirst O(n), addLast O(1) amortised

For freshers: Two readable shortcuts: addFirst(x) means add(0, x) and addLast(x) means add(x). They arrived in Java 21 with the new SequencedCollection interface.

For experienced developers: They are default methods that every List now has, so code that needs "first/last" semantics can accept any sequenced collection. On an ArrayList, addFirst still shifts every element.

Reading elements

Reading never changes the list. Use get for a position, indexOf to find a value, and contains to ask "is it there?".

get(int index)

  • Signature: E get(int index)
  • Returns: the element at that index
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Returns the element at the given index. Indexes start at 0, so the third fort is get(2). An index below 0 or at/above size() throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

For experienced developers: Direct array access after a bounds check: this is why ArrayList is the default list. It is also why a for (int i...) loop with get(i) is perfectly fine on an ArrayList but slow (O(n²)) on a LinkedList.

getFirst() and getLast() (Java 21)

  • Signature: E getFirst(); E getLast()
  • Returns: the first / last element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read the first or the last element without writing get(0) or get(size() - 1). On an empty list they throw NoSuchElementException (unlike get(0), which throws IndexOutOfBoundsException).

For experienced developers: Part of SequencedCollection. They make the intent obvious and avoid the classic off-by-one mistake in size() - 1.

size() and isEmpty()

  • Signature: int size(); boolean isEmpty()
  • Returns: the number of elements / whether it has none
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: size() counts the elements that are really stored (not the capacity). isEmpty() is simply size() == 0; prefer it because it reads better.

For experienced developers: size is a plain int field, so both calls are free. Remember that size() is the number of elements, not the size of the internal array (that is the capacity).

contains(Object o)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: true if an equal element exists
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Answers "is this value in the list?". It checks the elements one by one from the start until it finds a match.

For experienced developers: Matching uses equals(), not ==, so your own classes must override equals (and hashCode) to be found. If you call contains often on a big list, use a HashSet instead (O(1)).

containsAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean containsAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if every element of c is present
  • Time: O(n*m)

For freshers: Checks that all of the given elements are in the list. Handy to test "does this route cover all the forts I want?".

For experienced developers: Implemented in AbstractCollection as a loop of contains calls, hence O(n*m). For big inputs, copy into a HashSet first.

indexOf(Object o) and lastIndexOf(Object o)

  • Signature: int indexOf(Object o); int lastIndexOf(Object o)
  • Returns: the index, or -1 if not found
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: indexOf gives the position of the first match, lastIndexOf the position of the last match. Because the list may contain duplicates, these can differ. If the value is missing you get -1.

For experienced developers: Both use equals(). A negative result is not an exception, so always test for -1 before using it as an index.

Changing elements

Replace one element, transform all elements, or put them in a new order. None of these change the size of the list.

set(int index, E e)

  • Signature: E set(int index, E element)
  • Returns: the element that was replaced
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Overwrites the element at index with a new one and gives you the old element back. The size does not change (unlike add(i, e), which inserts).

For experienced developers: A plain array store after a bounds check; it does not increase modCount, so it is allowed while you iterate (it is not a structural change).

replaceAll(UnaryOperator op)

  • Signature: void replaceAll(UnaryOperator operator)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Applies a function to every element and stores the result back in the same position, for example "make every name upper case". Write the function as a lambda: s -> s.toUpperCase().

For experienced developers: Runs in place and does not create a second list. The operator must return the same type (UnaryOperator<E>). It is a cleaner alternative to a for loop that calls set for each index.

sort(Comparator c)

  • Signature: void sort(Comparator c)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sorts the list in place. Pass null (or Comparator.naturalOrder()) for natural order: A to Z for text, small to large for numbers. Pass your own comparator for any other order, for example by length.

For experienced developers: Uses TimSort, which is stable (equal elements keep their relative order) and very fast on partly sorted data. Collections.sort(list) simply calls list.sort(null). Elements must be mutually comparable or you must supply a comparator, otherwise ClassCastException.

Collections.reverse, swap and shuffle

  • Signature: Collections.reverse(List); Collections.swap(List, int, int); Collections.shuffle(List)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: The Collections helper class (note the s) works on any list: reverse flips the order, swap exchanges two positions, shuffle randomises the order.

For experienced developers: They change the list in place. shuffle accepts a Random; passing a seeded new Random(42) makes the shuffle repeatable, which is what you want in tests. In Java 21 list.reversed() gives a reversed view without copying.

Removing elements

There are many ways to remove. Pick by what you know: the position, the value, a group of values, or a rule.

remove(int index) and remove(Object o)

  • Signature: E remove(int index); boolean remove(Object o)
  • Returns: the removed element / true if something was removed
  • Time: O(n): later elements shift left

For freshers: remove(index) removes by position and returns the removed element. remove(value) removes the first element equal to the value and returns true or false. After a removal the elements after it move one step left, so their indexes change.

For experienced developers: With List<Integer> the call list.remove(2) is remove by index, because int matches remove(int) exactly. To remove the value 2 you must write list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)). This trap catches many developers (see the example).

Watch out: Removing inside a plain for or for-each loop skips elements or throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use removeIf or an Iterator (shown below).

removeAll(Collection c) and retainAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean removeAll(Collection c); boolean retainAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the list changed
  • Time: O(n*m)

For freshers: removeAll(c) deletes every element that is in c (a "subtract"). retainAll(c) keeps only the elements that are in c and deletes the rest (an "intersection").

For experienced developers: Both run a single pass over the list, calling c.contains(...) for each element. Make c a HashSet when it is large, otherwise the cost is O(n*m).

removeIf(Predicate p)

  • Signature: boolean removeIf(Predicate filter)
  • Returns: true if anything was removed
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Removes every element that matches a rule. The rule is a lambda that returns true for the elements to delete, e.g. n -> n % 2 == 0 for "all even numbers". It is the safe and short way to remove while looping.

For experienced developers: ArrayList overrides it with a one-pass bit-set algorithm: it first marks the elements to delete, then compacts the array once, so it is O(n) instead of O(n²) for repeated remove calls. It also checks modCount and throws ConcurrentModificationException if the predicate itself modifies the list.

removeFirst() and removeLast() (Java 21)

  • Signature: E removeFirst(); E removeLast()
  • Returns: the removed element
  • Time: removeFirst O(n), removeLast O(1)

For freshers: Take the first or last element out of the list and return it. On an empty list they throw NoSuchElementException.

For experienced developers: Together with addLast they let an ArrayList act as a stack (use the end) efficiently. For a queue (taking from the front) the shifting makes it O(n); use ArrayDeque for that.

clear()

  • Signature: void clear()
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Removes all elements. The list object is still there and still usable; its size becomes 0.

For experienced developers: It sets every slot to null so the removed objects can be garbage collected, but it keeps the internal array, so the capacity stays. To release the memory too, call trimToSize() afterwards or drop the list.

Parts, copies and conversions

Sometimes you need a piece of a list, a copy, an array, a stream or a read-only version.

subList(int from, int to)

  • Signature: List subList(int fromIndex, int toIndex)
  • Returns: a view of that range
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Gives you the part of the list from from (included) up to to (excluded). It is not a copy: it is a window onto the original list, so changing the window changes the list and the other way round.

For experienced developers: The view keeps a reference to its parent. If you change the parent's size (add or remove) after creating the view and then use the view, you get ConcurrentModificationException. Clearing a sub-list is a neat way to delete a range in one call: list.subList(2, 5).clear(). Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(list.subList(...)) when you want an independent copy.

toArray()

  • Signature: Object[] toArray(); T[] toArray(T[] a)
  • Returns: an array holding the elements
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Copies the list into an array, for old APIs that need an array. toArray() returns an Object[]. To get a String[] pass an empty array of that type: list.toArray(new String[0]).

For experienced developers: The copy is independent of the list (changing one does not change the other); the elements themselves are the same objects. Since Java 11 you can also write list.toArray(String[]::new). Passing a zero-length array is the recommended style: it is as fast as pre-sizing and safer.

stream()

  • Signature: Stream stream()
  • Returns: a stream over the elements
  • Time: O(1) to create; O(n) to process

For freshers: Starts a pipeline to filter, change, count or collect the elements without writing loops: list.stream().filter(...).map(...).toList(). The original list is not changed.

For experienced developers: The stream is lazy and single-use. Because ArrayList is RandomAccess and sized, its spliterator splits evenly, so parallelStream() can be effective for large, CPU-heavy work (but measure first).

List.of, List.copyOf and Arrays.asList

  • Signature: List.of(E...); List.copyOf(Collection); Arrays.asList(T...)
  • Returns: a read-only or fixed-size list (not an ArrayList)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Three quick ways to create a list from values. List.of(...) and List.copyOf(...) give an immutable list (no add, remove or set at all, and no null). Arrays.asList(...) gives a fixed-size list: you may set but not add or remove.

For experienced developers: None of them is a java.util.ArrayList (Arrays.asList returns a private inner class that writes through to the array). Wrap in new ArrayList<>(...) when you need a normal mutable list.

Watch out: A very common bug is Arrays.asList(...).add(...): it compiles, then fails at run time.

Collections.unmodifiableList and synchronizedList

  • Signature: Collections.unmodifiableList(List); Collections.synchronizedList(List)
  • Returns: a wrapper view of the same list
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: unmodifiableList hands out a read-only view (safe to give to other code). synchronizedList wraps the list so that each single method call is thread-safe.

For experienced developers: Both are views: the unmodifiable view still shows later changes made through the original list, so it is not an immutable snapshot (use List.copyOf for that). A synchronized list still needs a manual synchronized (list) { ... } block while iterating.

clone() and the copy constructor

  • Signature: Object clone(); new ArrayList<>(Collection)
  • Returns: a shallow copy of the list
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Both create a new list with the same elements. Adding or removing in the copy does not affect the original. But the elements are shared: a shallow copy does not duplicate the objects inside.

For experienced developers: Prefer the copy constructor: it needs no cast and no @SuppressWarnings. If the elements are mutable objects and you need independent data, you must copy each element yourself (a deep copy).

equals, hashCode and toString

  • Signature: boolean equals(Object o); int hashCode(); String toString()
  • Returns: content-based comparison, hash and text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Two lists are equal when they have the same elements in the same order. toString() prints [a, b, c]. hashCode() is computed from the elements, so equal lists have equal hash codes.

For experienced developers: Because the hash depends on the contents, never use a mutable list as a key in a HashMap or as an element of a HashSet if you will change it afterwards. A list is equal to any other List implementation with the same contents (an ArrayList equals a LinkedList holding the same elements).

Walking through the list (iteration)

There are five common ways to visit every element. Each has a best use.

for loop and for-each loop

  • Signature: for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) ...; for (E e : list) ...
  • Returns: one element per step
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Use the for-each loop when you just need to read every element: it is short and cannot go out of range. Use the index loop when you need the position, or need to change elements with set.

For experienced developers: The for-each loop is compiled to an Iterator, so it is fail-fast. The index loop has no such check, which is why removing inside it silently skips the element after each removed one.

iterator()

  • Signature: Iterator iterator()
  • Returns: an iterator (hasNext, next, remove)
  • Time: O(1) per step

For freshers: An Iterator is a bookmark that walks the list one element at a time. hasNext() asks "is there another element?", next() returns it, and remove() deletes the element that next() just returned. It is the classic way to remove while looping.

For experienced developers: The ArrayList iterator is fail-fast: it remembers modCount and throws ConcurrentModificationException if the list is changed by anything other than the iterator's own remove(). remove() may be called only once per next().

listIterator() and listIterator(int index)

  • Signature: ListIterator listIterator(); ListIterator listIterator(int index)
  • Returns: an iterator that moves both ways
  • Time: O(1) per step

For freshers: A ListIterator is an Iterator that can also go backwards (hasPrevious, previous), tell the index (nextIndex, previousIndex), replace the last returned element (set) and insert a new element at the cursor (add).

For experienced developers: It is the only tool that lets you insert or replace safely while walking a list. listIterator(size()) starts at the end for a reverse walk.

forEach(Consumer)

  • Signature: void forEach(Consumer action)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Runs one action for every element, written as a lambda or a method reference: forts.forEach(System.out::println). It is short and reads well for simple tasks.

For experienced developers: ArrayList's version loops over the internal array directly and checks modCount once at the end, so it is slightly faster than an iterator. You cannot use break or continue inside it; use a normal loop when you need them.

Fail-fast: ConcurrentModificationException

  • Signature: modCount check inside Iterator / for-each
  • Returns: throws ConcurrentModificationException
  • Time: -

For freshers: If you add or remove elements while a for-each loop is running, Java stops with ConcurrentModificationException. It protects you from a half-updated loop. The fix is to remove with an Iterator, with removeIf, or to loop over a copy.

For experienced developers: Fail-fast is best-effort (a debugging aid), not a guarantee for multi-threaded use. Quirk: removing the second last element in a for-each loop ends the loop without an error because hasNext() becomes false first. Do not rely on that.

Capacity: ensureCapacity and trimToSize

ArrayList has two sizes: size (how many elements it holds) and capacity (how many fit before it must grow). These two methods manage the second one.

ensureCapacity(int) and trimToSize()

  • Signature: void ensureCapacity(int minCapacity); void trimToSize()
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: ensureCapacity(n) makes room for at least n elements in one go, which is faster if you are about to add many elements. trimToSize() cuts the unused room so the list uses the least memory. Neither changes size() or the elements.

For experienced developers: They exist only on ArrayList (not on the List interface). Use ensureCapacity before a big bulk load, and trimToSize after a list has become final and long-lived. The capacity cannot be read through the public API; the program below shows the growth rule with arithmetic.

expert.content:
How ArrayList works inside

Knowing the internals explains every number in the method tables.

  • The data lives in transient Object[] elementData. size is a separate int; slots from size to the end of the array are unused (and set to null).
  • new ArrayList<>() shares a tiny static empty array; the first add allocates an array of 10. With new ArrayList<>(n) it allocates exactly n slots (and n = 0 gives the shared empty array).
  • When the array is full, grow computes newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1) (about 1.5×) and copies with Arrays.copyOf. The growth steps are 10, 15, 22, 33, 49, 73, ...
  • Inserting or removing in the middle calls System.arraycopy to shift the tail: a fast native block copy, but still O(n).
  • modCount (inherited from AbstractList) is increased on every structural change; iterators compare it to the value they saw when they started (fail-fast).
  • The maximum size is about Integer.MAX_VALUE - 8; beyond that you get OutOfMemoryError.

Time complexity summary

OperationCostWhy
get(i), set(i, e), size(), isEmpty()O(1)Direct array access
add(e) / addLast(e)O(1) amortisedWrites the next slot; sometimes one O(n) growth
add(i, e), remove(i), addFirst, removeFirstO(n)Shifts every element after i
removeLast()O(1)No shifting needed
contains, indexOf, remove(Object)O(n)Linear search with equals()
addAll(c)O(m)One bulk copy
sortO(n log n)TimSort (stable)
iterator step, listIterator stepO(1)Index into the array
subList(a, b)O(1)Creates a view, no copy
clear()O(n)Nulls every slot so the objects can be collected

Traps that surprise even experienced developers

Each trap below has a runnable proof.

Trap 1: contains, indexOf and remove(Object) depend on equals()

  • A plain class without equals compares by identity, so two objects with the same data are "different".
  • A record gets a content-based equals for free.
  • If you override equals, also override hashCode (needed the moment the object goes into a HashSet or HashMap).

Trap 2: Integer objects and ==

  • Values between -128 and 127 are cached, so == happens to work for small numbers and fails for bigger ones.
  • Always compare wrapper objects with equals() (or unbox first).

Trap 3: subList is a view

  • Changing the parent's size after creating a view, then using the view, throws ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Copy the view into a new list when you need to keep it: new ArrayList<>(list.subList(a, b)).

Thread safety

ArrayList is not thread-safe. Two threads adding at the same time can lose elements, throw exceptions or corrupt the list. Pick one of these:

Choosing a thread-safe list

ChoiceHow it worksUse when
Collections.synchronizedList(list)One lock around every methodLight sharing; you must still lock manually while iterating
CopyOnWriteArrayListEvery write copies the whole array; readers never block and never see a change in the middle of a loopMany reads, very few writes (listeners, configuration)
VectorOld class, synchronized methodsLegacy code only; prefer the two above
Confine to one thread / immutable List.copyOfNo sharing, no problemBest of all when possible

ArrayList compared with other lists

ArrayListLinkedListVectorCopyOnWriteArrayList
InsideResizable arrayDoubly linked nodesResizable arrayArray copied on each write
get(i)O(1)O(n)O(1)O(1)
add at endO(1) amortisedO(1)O(1) amortisedO(n)
insert / remove in the middleO(n) shift (fast native copy)O(1) once positioned, O(n) to find the positionO(n)O(n)
MemoryCompactAbout 24 extra bytes per elementCompactCompact (+ copies)
Thread-safeNoNoYes (every method locked)Yes
Typical useDefault choiceQueue / deque use, rarely a listLegacyRead-mostly shared data

In practice ArrayList wins in almost every benchmark, even for middle inserts, because arrays are cache-friendly and System.arraycopy is very fast. Choose another list only for a clear reason.

Best practices

Habits that make ArrayList code correct, fast and easy to read.

  • Declare with the interface: List<String> forts = new ArrayList<>();.
  • Pass an initial capacity (new ArrayList<>(expectedSize)) when you know the size, to skip repeated growth.
  • Use removeIf, replaceAll and forEach instead of hand-written loops for simple jobs.
  • Never remove inside a for-each loop. Use removeIf or an Iterator.
  • Return a copy or an unmodifiable view from your getters (List.copyOf(list)) so callers cannot change your internal list.
  • Do not store null unless you have to; many APIs (List.of, streams) reject it.
  • For millions of numbers prefer a primitive array or a primitive collection library: ArrayList<Integer> boxes every value (about 16 bytes per Integer plus the reference).
  • Write equals and hashCode for your element classes (or use record) so contains, indexOf and remove(Object) behave.
  • Prefer list.sort(comparator) to hand-written sorting, and keep comparators consistent with equals when you can.

Real example: a pilgrim route planner

One program that uses many of the methods together: build a route, insert and remove stops, sort, search and copy.

interviewQA: What is an ArrayList and how is it different from an array?

An ArrayList is a resizable-array implementation of the List interface. An array has a fixed length and can hold primitives; an ArrayList grows and shrinks, holds only objects (wrapper types for numbers) and provides methods such as add, remove, contains and sort. Both give O(1) access by index.
How does ArrayList grow? What is the default capacity?

It keeps an Object[]. new ArrayList<>() starts with a shared empty array and allocates 10 slots on the first add. When full it grows to oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1), about 1.5 times, using Arrays.copyOf. That is why add is amortised O(1).
Time complexity of get, add, add(index), remove(index), contains?
get O(1); add at end O(1) amortised; add(index) and remove(index) O(n) because later elements are shifted; contains and indexOf O(n) because they scan with equals().
ArrayList vs LinkedList: which should you choose?

ArrayList by default: O(1) get, compact memory and very fast bulk copies. LinkedList only as a queue/deque (add/remove at both ends); its O(n) get and per-node overhead make it slower as a general list.
ArrayList vs Vector?

Both use a growable array. Vector synchronizes every method and doubles its capacity by default; ArrayList is unsynchronized, grows by 1.5x and is faster. For thread safety use Collections.synchronizedList or CopyOnWriteArrayList instead of Vector.
Is ArrayList thread-safe? How do you make it safe?
No. Use Collections.synchronizedList (and synchronize manually while iterating), CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly data, or avoid sharing the list between threads.
What is fail-fast behaviour?

ArrayList iterators remember modCount. If the list is structurally modified by anything other than the iterator itself, the next iterator call throws ConcurrentModificationException. It is a best-effort bug detector, not a thread-safety guarantee.
How do you remove elements safely while iterating?
Use Iterator.remove(), ListIterator, removeIf(predicate), or iterate over a copy. Do not call list.remove inside a for-each loop.
What does list.remove(2) do on a List<Integer>?
It calls remove(int index) and removes the element at index 2. To remove the value 2 write list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)).
What is the difference between size and capacity?
size is the number of elements stored; capacity is the length of the internal array. Capacity is always at least size. ensureCapacity and trimToSize manage the capacity.
Does ArrayList allow duplicates and null?
Yes to both. It keeps insertion order and allows any number of duplicates and nulls.
Why does Arrays.asList(...).add(...) throw an exception?
Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list backed by the array: set is allowed but add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(...) for a growable list.
What is the difference between clone() and the copy constructor? Is it a deep copy?

Both create a new list with the same element references (a shallow copy): changing the list structure does not affect the original, but the element objects are shared. For a deep copy you must copy each element yourself.
How does contains() find an element?

It scans from index 0 and compares with equals(). Elements of your own classes need a proper equals (and hashCode) or the search will not find equal-looking objects. For frequent lookups use a HashSet.
Why is subList called a view and what can go wrong?

It returns a window onto the same backing array, so writes through the view affect the original and vice versa. If you add or remove in the original after creating the view, using the view throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copy it with new ArrayList<>(list.subList(a, b)) if you need a snapshot.
How do you sort an ArrayList, and is the sort stable?
list.sort(comparator) or Collections.sort(list). It uses TimSort, which is stable and O(n log n), and fast on partly ordered data.
What new List methods does Java 21 add?
getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed, from the new SequencedCollection interface that List now extends.

beginner.content:
What is a LinkedList?

A LinkedList stores its elements in separate little objects called nodes. Every node holds one element and two links: one to the previous node and one to the next node. Picture a chain of forts connected by roads in both directions: to go from the first fort to the fourth you must walk through the second and the third. There is no numbered shelf like in an array.

  • It lives in java.util. It implements List (indexes, order), Deque and Queue (work at both ends).
  • Fast at the two ends: adding or removing the first or last element changes only a couple of links: O(1).
  • Slow in the middle: get(i) has to walk from the nearest end to position i: O(n).
  • No capacity and no resizing: the list simply gets one more node when you add.
  • Keeps insertion order, allows duplicates and null, and is not thread-safe.
  • Each element costs extra memory for its node (about 24 bytes on a typical JVM) compared with an ArrayList.

Where LinkedList sits in the Collection Framework

(I) = interface, (c) = class. LinkedList also implements Deque (which extends Queue), Cloneable and Serializable. It does not implement RandomAccess, because index access is not fast.

How the nodes are linked

Inside, a LinkedList keeps only three fields: first (the first node), last (the last node) and size.

To insert a new fort after Node 1, Java creates one new node and re-points two links on each side. Nothing else moves. That is why inserting is cheap once you are at the right place, and finding that place is the expensive part.

Creating a LinkedList

  • new LinkedList<>(): an empty list.
  • new LinkedList<>(Collection c): a list holding the elements of another collection, in its iteration order.
  • There is no capacity constructor, because a linked list has no capacity.
  • Declare the variable as List, Queue or Deque depending on how you will use it.

All LinkedList methods at a glance

intermediate.content:
Adding elements

LinkedList gives you many names for "add at an end". The names come from the three roles the class plays: List, Queue and Deque.

add, addLast and offer

  • Signature: boolean add(E e); void addLast(E e); boolean offer(E e)
  • Returns: add and offer return true; addLast returns nothing
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: All three put the element at the end of the list. Use add when you think "list", offer when you think "queue", and addLast when you think "deque".

For experienced developers: They all call the same internal linkLast: create a node, point the old last node's next at it, and update last. A LinkedList has no capacity limit, so offer never returns false here (it can for bounded queues).

addFirst, push and offerFirst

  • Signature: void addFirst(E e); void push(E e); boolean offerFirst(E e)
  • Returns: nothing / nothing / true
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: These put the element at the front. Adding at the front is where LinkedList beats ArrayList: no shifting. push is the name used when the list acts like a stack (last in, first out).

For experienced developers: push(e) is just addFirst(e). Together with pop() (which removes the first element) you get a stack that is consistent with the Deque contract. Note: the legacy Stack class works at the other end and is synchronized.

add(int index, E e)

  • Signature: void add(int index, E element)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n) to reach the index

For freshers: Inserts the element at a position. Linking the new node is instant, but Java must first walk to that position, one node at a time.

For experienced developers: The walk starts from whichever end is closer (index < size/2 goes from the front, otherwise from the back), so the average cost is about n/4 steps. For an insertion that is far from both ends an ArrayList is usually still faster because its shifting is a native block copy.

addAll(Collection c) and addAll(int index, Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean addAll(Collection c); boolean addAll(int index, Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the list changed
  • Time: O(m) / O(index + m)

For freshers: Adds all elements of another collection, at the end or starting at an index, keeping their order.

For experienced developers: It converts the argument to an array, then links the new nodes in one pass, so it is efficient even for the indexed version (only one walk to the index).

Reading elements

Reading the ends is O(1). Reading in the middle walks the chain. Pick the variant by what you want when the list is empty: an exception or null.

getFirst, getLast and element

  • Signature: E getFirst(); E getLast(); E element()
  • Returns: the element at that end
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read the first or last element without removing it. On an empty list they throw NoSuchElementException. element() is the queue name for getFirst().

For experienced developers: They read the first / last pointers directly. If an empty list is normal in your program, use the peek family (next card), which returns null instead of throwing.

peek, peekFirst and peekLast

  • Signature: E peek(); E peekFirst(); E peekLast()
  • Returns: the element, or null if the list is empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Look at an end without removing it; if the list is empty you get null, not an exception. peek() and peekFirst() look at the front, peekLast() at the back.

For experienced developers: These are the "safe" counterparts of getFirst/getLast. Because LinkedList allows null elements, a null result is ambiguous: it could be "empty" or "the element is null". Check isEmpty() if you store nulls.

get(int index) and set(int index, E e)

  • Signature: E get(int index); E set(int index, E element)
  • Returns: the element / the replaced element
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Read or replace by position. It works, but remember the list has to walk to the index: reading the 500th element touches up to 250 nodes.

For experienced developers: The cost is why a for (int i...) list.get(i) loop over a LinkedList is O(n²). Use a for-each loop or an iterator instead: they move from one node to the next in O(1) per step.

contains, indexOf and lastIndexOf

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o); int indexOf(Object o); int lastIndexOf(Object o)
  • Returns: true / the index / the index (or -1)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Search by value from the front (indexOf, contains) or from the back (lastIndexOf). Matching uses equals().

For experienced developers: Linear scans, identical in behaviour to ArrayList. Override equals in your element class (or use a record) so the search works for your objects.

Removing elements

Removing an end is O(1). The names differ again by what happens on an empty list.

remove(), removeFirst, pop and removeLast

  • Signature: E remove(); E removeFirst(); E pop(); E removeLast()
  • Returns: the removed element (throws on an empty list)
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: remove(), removeFirst() and pop() all take the first element out and return it; removeLast() takes the last. If the list is empty they throw NoSuchElementException.

For experienced developers: The no-argument remove() is the Queue method and must not be confused with remove(int) / remove(Object). Removing an end only updates one or two links, with no shifting.

poll, pollFirst and pollLast

  • Signature: E poll(); E pollFirst(); E pollLast()
  • Returns: the removed element, or null if empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Like remove, but safe: when the list is empty you get null instead of an exception. poll() is the standard way to take the next item from a queue in a loop: while ((x = queue.poll()) != null).

For experienced developers: Prefer poll in queue-style code and removeFirst when an empty list would be a bug that you want to see as an exception.

remove(int index) and remove(Object o)

  • Signature: E remove(int index); boolean remove(Object o)
  • Returns: the removed element / true if found
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Remove by position or by value (the first equal element). Both have to walk the chain to find the node, then unlink it.

For experienced developers: The same overload trap exists as in ArrayList: on a LinkedList<Integer>, remove(2) removes index 2; use remove(Integer.valueOf(2)) for the value. removeFirstOccurrence and removeLastOccurrence (next card) make the direction explicit.

removeFirstOccurrence and removeLastOccurrence

  • Signature: boolean removeFirstOccurrence(Object o); boolean removeLastOccurrence(Object o)
  • Returns: true if an element was removed
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Remove the first or the last element equal to the value, when the list holds duplicates.

For experienced developers: removeFirstOccurrence is the same as remove(Object). removeLastOccurrence scans from the back, which is the only direct way to remove the last match in a list.

removeIf, removeAll, retainAll and clear

  • Signature: boolean removeIf(Predicate); boolean removeAll(Collection); boolean retainAll(Collection); void clear()
  • Returns: true if changed / nothing
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Remove by a rule, remove everything found in another collection, keep only what is found in another collection, or remove everything.

For experienced developers: These are inherited from Collection; they work with an iterator, unlinking nodes as they go. clear() unlinks every node (setting their fields to null to help the garbage collector).

Using LinkedList as a Queue, a Stack and a Deque

Because LinkedList is also a Deque, the same object can be used three ways. Choose the interface type that matches your use so the code says what you mean.

The same LinkedList as Queue, Stack and Deque

RoleAddRemoveLookOrder
Queue (line at a ticket window)offer(e) at the backpoll() from the frontpeek()First in, first out (FIFO)
Stack (pile of plates)push(e) on top (front)pop() from the top (front)peek()Last in, first out (LIFO)
Deque (both ends)offerFirst / offerLastpollFirst / pollLastpeekFirst / peekLastBoth ends

For pure queue or stack work, ArrayDeque is usually even faster (no node objects), but it does not allow null and has no index methods.

Changing, converting and walking

The rest of the List API works exactly as in ArrayList, so only the LinkedList-specific points are shown here.

iterator, listIterator and descendingIterator

  • Signature: Iterator iterator(); ListIterator listIterator(); Iterator descendingIterator()
  • Returns: an iterator
  • Time: O(1) per step

For freshers: Walk the list element by element. iterator() goes forward, listIterator() also goes backward and can add or replace, and descendingIterator() walks from the last element to the first. Iterators are the right way to loop a LinkedList because each step is O(1).

For experienced developers: The iterators are fail-fast (they check modCount). A ListIterator can insert in the middle in O(1) at the cursor: this is the one case where LinkedList truly beats ArrayList for middle insertion, because you are already standing on the node.

sort, replaceAll, forEach, stream, toArray, subList

  • Signature: inherited from List and Collection
  • Returns: as for ArrayList
  • Time: O(n) or O(n log n)

For freshers: These work just like on an ArrayList: sort orders the list, replaceAll changes every element, forEach runs an action, stream starts a pipeline, toArray copies into an array and subList gives a range view.

For experienced developers: sort copies the nodes into an array, sorts it with TimSort and writes the values back, so there is no benefit from being a linked list. If you sort a lot, you probably wanted an ArrayList.

clone, equals, hashCode, toString and reversed

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString(); LinkedList reversed()
  • Returns: a shallow copy / comparisons / text / a reversed view
  • Time: O(n) / O(1)

For freshers: clone() makes a shallow copy (the new list has its own nodes but shares the elements). Two lists are equals when they have the same elements in the same order, whatever the list class. In Java 21 reversed() gives a view that walks from the back.

For experienced developers: Prefer the copy constructor over clone(). A reversed view is not a copy: changes through it change the original.

expert.content:
How LinkedList works inside

A short tour of the source code explains every cost in the tables.

  • The class keeps transient int size, Node<E> first and Node<E> last. Each Node has item, next and prev.
  • linkLast(e): create a node whose prev is the old last; set last to it; link the old last's next; size++; modCount++. No arrays, no copying, so no "amortised" caveat.
  • node(index) picks the nearest end: if index < (size >> 1) it walks from first via next, otherwise from last via prev. That is why access in the middle is the slowest.
  • unlink(node) reconnects the neighbours and clears the node's fields so the garbage collector can reclaim it.
  • Memory: on a 64-bit JVM with compressed pointers a node is 24 bytes (12 header + 3 references x 4). A million elements cost 24 MB of nodes on top of the elements themselves, versus 4 MB of references in an ArrayList.
  • Cache behaviour: nodes are scattered in memory, so walking a LinkedList causes many CPU cache misses, while an ArrayList reads contiguous memory. This is why ArrayList often wins even where Big-O suggests otherwise.

Time complexity summary

OperationLinkedListArrayList (for comparison)
get(i), set(i, e)O(n), up to n/2 stepsO(1)
add at the endO(1)O(1) amortised
add / remove at the frontO(1)O(n)
add(i, e), remove(i) in the middleO(n) to reach i, then O(1) to linkO(n) shift (fast block copy)
Insert / remove through a ListIterator at the cursorO(1)O(n)
contains, indexOfO(n)O(n)
Memory per element~24 bytes node + element~4 bytes reference + element
Iteration speedSlower (cache misses)Faster

Trap: indexed loops are quadratic

  • A for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) list.get(i) loop calls get n times, each costing up to n/2 steps: O(n²).
  • Use a for-each loop, an Iterator, or forEach: O(n) in total.
  • The program below counts node visits to make the difference visible without timing.

LinkedList vs ArrayList vs ArrayDeque: which one?

NeedBest choiceWhy
A general list you read by indexArrayListO(1) get, compact, cache-friendly
A queue or a stackArrayDequeNo node objects, faster than LinkedList; no nulls
A queue that must hold null, or needs both the List and Deque APIsLinkedListThe only class that is both a List and a Deque
Many inserts/removals through an iterator in the middle of a big listLinkedListO(1) at the cursor
Thread-safe queueConcurrentLinkedDeque / LinkedBlockingDequeLinkedList is not synchronized

Rule of thumb: start with ArrayList, and move to ArrayDeque for queues and stacks. LinkedList is a niche choice.

Best practices

Habits that keep LinkedList code correct and fast.

  • Declare the variable as the interface you use: Queue<T>, Deque<T> or List<T>.
  • Never loop with get(i); use for-each, an iterator or a stream.
  • Use the poll/peek/offer family when "empty" is a normal state, and remove/get/add when it would be a bug.
  • Avoid null elements, because peek()/poll() use null to mean "empty".
  • For thread safety use ConcurrentLinkedDeque or wrap with Collections.synchronizedList; remember to lock while iterating.
  • Do not use LinkedList only because "insertion is O(1)": measure first; ArrayList is faster for most sizes.

Real example: a ticket counter with undo

A queue of travellers and a stack of cancelled tickets, both built on LinkedList.

interviewQA: What is a LinkedList and how is it different from an ArrayList?

LinkedList is a doubly linked list: each element sits in a node with prev and next references. It gives O(1) insertion and removal at both ends and via an iterator, but O(n) index access. ArrayList uses an array: O(1) index access, O(n) insert/remove in the middle and at the front.
Which interfaces does LinkedList implement?
List, Deque (and so Queue), Cloneable and Serializable. It does not implement RandomAccess.
Time complexity of get(i), add at the end, add at the front, remove in the middle?
get(i) O(n) (walks from the nearer end); add at end O(1); add/remove at the front O(1); remove(index) O(n) to find the node, then O(1) to unlink.
When would you actually choose LinkedList?

When you need both List and Deque behaviour in one object, need to store nulls in a queue, or do many insertions/removals through a ListIterator in a large list. For plain queues and stacks ArrayDeque is better; for general lists ArrayList is better.
Why is a for loop with get(i) slow on a LinkedList?
Each get(i) walks the chain, so n calls cost O(n^2). Use for-each, an Iterator or streams, which move node to node in O(1).
Difference between remove(), poll() and pop()?
remove() and pop() take the first element and throw NoSuchElementException when empty; poll() takes the first element and returns null when empty. pop() is the stack name for removeFirst().
What is the difference between peek() and element()?
Both read the head without removing it; peek() returns null for an empty list, element() throws NoSuchElementException.
How do you use LinkedList as a stack?
Declare Deque<T> stack = new LinkedList<>(); use push(e) to add on top, pop() to remove from the top and peek() to look. They all work at the front of the list.
Does LinkedList allow duplicates and null?
Yes. Be careful with null because peek() and poll() return null to signal an empty list.
Is LinkedList thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentLinkedDeque or LinkedBlockingDeque for concurrent use, or wrap with Collections.synchronizedList and synchronise manually while iterating.
What is the memory overhead of LinkedList?
Each element needs a Node object: about 24 bytes (object header plus three references) on a 64-bit JVM with compressed pointers, compared with a 4-byte reference slot in an ArrayList.
How does node(index) decide where to start walking?
If index is less than size/2 it walks forward from first, otherwise it walks backward from last, so it needs at most about n/2 steps.
What does descendingIterator() do?
It returns an iterator that visits the elements from last to first, without creating a reversed copy.
Why can ListIterator.add() be O(1) on a LinkedList?
The iterator already holds a reference to the neighbouring nodes, so inserting a new node only changes the links around the cursor; no search is needed.
