beginner.content:
What is a Vector?

A Vector is a resizable array, just like ArrayList, with one big difference: every method is synchronized, so only one thread at a time can use it. It is one of the oldest classes of Java (from version 1.0, before the Collection Framework existed) and was later retrofitted to implement List.

  • Package java.util. Implements List, RandomAccess, Cloneable, Serializable.
  • Keeps insertion order, allows duplicates and null, and reads by index in O(1).
  • Thread-safe because each method locks the vector. This makes it slower than ArrayList when only one thread is used.
  • Default capacity is 10. When full it doubles its capacity (or grows by a fixed capacityIncrement if you set one).
  • Has many old-style methods (addElement, elementAt, removeElement, elements()) next to the modern List methods.
  • Modern advice: use ArrayList for single-threaded code, and CopyOnWriteArrayList or Collections.synchronizedList when you need thread safety. Learn Vector mainly to read old code and for interviews.

Where Vector sits in the Collection Framework

Iterable
(I)
← extends
Collection
(I)
← extends
List
(I)
← implements
AbstractList
(c)
← extends
Vector
(c)
← extends
Stack
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. Stack is a subclass of Vector, so it inherits all the Vector methods and the synchronization.

Creating a Vector: four constructors

  • new Vector<>(): empty, capacity 10, doubles when full.
  • new Vector<>(int initialCapacity): empty with the given capacity, doubles when full.
  • new Vector<>(int initialCapacity, int capacityIncrement): grows by that fixed amount instead of doubling.
  • new Vector<>(Collection c): a copy of another collection.

All Vector methods at a glance

n is the number of elements. The first group is the classic Vector API; the second is the List API that Vector shares with ArrayList.

MethodWhat it doesTime
addElement(e)Adds at the end (old name of add)O(1) amortised
insertElementAt(e, i)Inserts at index iO(n)
elementAt(i) / firstElement() / lastElement()Reads by index / first / lastO(1)
setElementAt(e, i)Replaces the element at iO(1)
removeElement(o) / removeElementAt(i) / removeAllElements()Removes by value / index / everythingO(n)
capacity() / ensureCapacity(n) / trimToSize() / setSize(n)Capacity management (setSize pads with null or truncates)O(1) / O(n)
elements()An old-style Enumeration (not fail-fast)O(1)
copyInto(Object[])Copies the elements into an arrayO(n)
indexOf(o, from) / lastIndexOf(o, from)Search starting at a given indexO(n)
add, get, set, remove, contains, size, clear, addAll, removeAll, retainAll ...The ordinary List methods, all synchronizedas ArrayList
sort, forEach, removeIf, replaceAll, stream, subList, iterator, listIteratorInherited List helpersas ArrayList

intermediate.content:
Adding and reading with the classic Vector methods

These names come from before Java 1.2. They still work and you will meet them in older code.

addElement, insertElementAt and add

  • Signature: void addElement(E obj); void insertElementAt(E obj, int index); boolean add(E e)
  • Returns: nothing / nothing / true
  • Time: O(1) amortised / O(n)

For freshers: addElement(x) and add(x) both append at the end. insertElementAt(x, i) puts x at index i and shifts the rest right. Note the argument order: element first, then index (the opposite of add(int, E)).

For experienced developers: addElement is the original method; add was added for the List interface and simply calls the same code. Each call takes the vector's lock, so a loop of a million adds pays for a million lock operations (the JVM can often optimise this away, but the lock is still part of the contract).

elementAt, firstElement, lastElement and get

  • Signature: E elementAt(int index); E firstElement(); E lastElement(); E get(int index)
  • Returns: the element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read an element by position (elementAt = get) or read the first or last. firstElement() and lastElement() throw NoSuchElementException on an empty vector; a bad index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

For experienced developers: Note the exception type: Vector throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (a subclass of IndexOutOfBoundsException), while ArrayList throws a plain IndexOutOfBoundsException.

setElementAt and set

  • Signature: void setElementAt(E obj, int index); E set(int index, E element)
  • Returns: nothing / the old element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Replace the element at an index. setElementAt(element, index) returns nothing; set(index, element) returns the element it replaced.

For experienced developers: Again the classic method has the argument order (element, index), while the List method has (index, element). Mixing them up compiles when both are int and Integer-compatible types are used: be careful with Vector<Integer>.

Removing elements

Remove by value, by index, or everything.

removeElement, removeElementAt and removeAllElements

  • Signature: boolean removeElement(Object obj); void removeElementAt(int index); void removeAllElements()
  • Returns: true if found / nothing / nothing
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: removeElement(x) removes the first element equal to x and says whether it found one. removeElementAt(i) removes by index. removeAllElements() empties the vector (same as clear()).

For experienced developers: removeElement is the same as remove(Object). Later elements shift left. An invalid index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Capacity

A Vector has a size (elements stored) and a capacity (room available). Unlike ArrayList, Vector lets you read the capacity.

capacity, ensureCapacity, trimToSize and setSize

  • Signature: int capacity(); void ensureCapacity(int); void trimToSize(); void setSize(int)
  • Returns: the capacity / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: capacity() tells how many elements fit before growing. ensureCapacity(n) makes room for n. trimToSize() shrinks the room to the size. setSize(n) changes the size itself: extra slots are filled with null, or elements beyond n are dropped.

For experienced developers: The growth rule is double the capacity (when no increment was given), not 1.5x as in ArrayList. setSize is a rare tool; it can create a vector full of nulls.

Searching

Besides the List search methods, Vector can start the search from a chosen index.

indexOf(o, from), lastIndexOf(o, from) and contains

  • Signature: int indexOf(Object o, int index); int lastIndexOf(Object o, int index); boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: the index (or -1) / true or false
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Search for a value starting at a position you choose: indexOf("Pune", 2) looks for Pune from index 2 onwards; lastIndexOf("Pune", 3) looks backwards from index 3.

For experienced developers: These two-argument searches exist only on Vector (not on ArrayList). Matching uses equals().

Walking through a Vector

Vector has two ways to walk that ArrayList does not mix: the old Enumeration and the modern Iterator.

elements() (Enumeration) versus iterator()

  • Signature: Enumeration elements(); Iterator iterator()
  • Returns: an Enumeration / an Iterator
  • Time: O(1) per step

For freshers: An Enumeration is the old way: hasMoreElements() and nextElement(). An Iterator is the new way: hasNext(), next() and remove(). Prefer Iterator (or for-each).

For experienced developers: The Vector Iterator is fail-fast (throws ConcurrentModificationException if the vector changes), but the Enumeration is not fail-fast and cannot remove. Both individual calls are synchronized, but a whole loop is not atomic: to iterate safely across threads you must synchronize on the vector yourself.

copyInto, toArray and clone

  • Signature: void copyInto(Object[] anArray); Object[] toArray(); Object clone()
  • Returns: nothing / an array / a shallow copy
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: copyInto(array) copies the elements into an array you provide (it must be big enough). toArray() creates a new array. clone() makes a shallow copy of the vector.

For experienced developers: copyInto is the classic method; toArray(new String[0]) is the modern equivalent that allocates the right array for you.

The inherited List methods

  • Signature: add, get, remove, contains, addAll, removeAll, retainAll, removeIf, replaceAll, sort, forEach, stream, subList, listIterator
  • Returns: as ArrayList
  • Time: as ArrayList

For freshers: Everything you learned for ArrayList also works on Vector: the same names, the same results. The only difference is that each call is synchronized.

For experienced developers: Because Vector implements List, you can swap new Vector<>() for new ArrayList<>() in most code by changing one word, provided you only used List methods (declare the variable as List to make that easy).

expert.content:
How Vector works inside

Vector and ArrayList are close relatives; the differences explain the behaviour.

  • Data lives in protected Object[] elementData with elementCount as the size. Both are protected, so subclasses (like Stack) can touch them.
  • Growth: newCapacity = oldCapacity + (capacityIncrement > 0 ? capacityIncrement : oldCapacity): it doubles unless you set an increment. ArrayList grows by half instead, so Vector may waste more memory.
  • Thread safety: methods are synchronized on the vector object. Single calls are atomic; compound actions are not: "if not contains then add" can still race between two threads.
  • Iterators are fail-fast via modCount; the old Enumeration is not.
  • Vector is never null-hostile: null elements are allowed.

Vector versus ArrayList

VectorArrayList
Thread safetyYes: every method is synchronizedNo
Speed (single thread)Slower (lock on each call)Faster
Growth when fullDoubles (or fixed increment)Grows by 50%
SinceJava 1.0 (retrofitted to List in 1.2)Java 1.2
Old methodsaddElement, elementAt, elements() ...None
IteratorsIterator (fail-fast) and Enumeration (not fail-fast)Iterator (fail-fast)
Read capacitycapacity()Not possible
TodayLegacyDefault list

The compound-action trap

  • Each Vector method is atomic, but a sequence of calls is not.
  • Checking contains and then calling add leaves a gap in which another thread can add the same value.
  • Lock around the whole sequence: synchronized (vector) { if (!vector.contains(x)) vector.add(x); }.
  • The sample shows the safe version (single-threaded, so it only proves the code runs; the point is the locking pattern).

Which list should you choose today?

SituationUseWhy
One thread (almost always)ArrayListNo locking cost
Read often, write rarely, shared by threadsCopyOnWriteArrayListReaders never block; no ConcurrentModificationException
Shared by threads with ordinary writesCollections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>())Same locking as Vector, but a modern API
Old code that already uses VectorKeep it, or migrate carefullyCheck for elements() and the Stack class

Best practices

Practical advice for the Vector you meet in real projects.

  • In new code avoid Vector and Stack; use ArrayList, ArrayDeque or a concurrent collection.
  • Declare variables as List so you can switch the implementation later.
  • Lock the vector (synchronized (v) {...}) around loops and check-then-act sequences that other threads can interleave.
  • Prefer iterator() or for-each to elements(); the Enumeration cannot remove and is not fail-fast.
  • Set the initial capacity if you know the size, to avoid repeated doubling.

Real example: a shared list of visited forts

Two worker threads add fort names to one Vector; the final size is always correct because each add is synchronized.

interviewQA: What is a Vector? Why is it called a legacy class?

Vector is a growable array from Java 1.0 whose methods are all synchronized. It was retrofitted to implement List in Java 1.2 but keeps old methods like addElement and elements(). It is called legacy because ArrayList and the concurrent collections replaced it.
Difference between Vector and ArrayList?

Vector is synchronized (thread-safe, slower), doubles its capacity when full and has the old Enumeration API; ArrayList is unsynchronized, grows by 50% and is the default choice for single-threaded code.
What is the default capacity of a Vector and how does it grow?
Capacity 10. When full it doubles, or grows by capacityIncrement if you passed one to the constructor.
Is Vector fully thread-safe?
Individual methods are atomic, but compound operations (check-then-act, iteration) are not, so you must lock the vector yourself around such sequences.
Enumeration versus Iterator on a Vector?
Enumeration (elements()) is the old read-only cursor and is not fail-fast; Iterator is the modern one, supports remove() and is fail-fast.
How do you make an ArrayList thread-safe instead of using Vector?
Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()), or CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly workloads.
What does setSize(n) do?
It changes the size of the vector: if n is larger the new slots are filled with null, if smaller the extra elements are discarded.
How does Vector relate to Stack?
Stack extends Vector, so a Stack is also synchronized and inherits every Vector method. Use ArrayDeque for a modern stack.
Does Vector allow null and duplicates?
Yes to both, and it keeps insertion order.
Which exception does elementAt(i) throw for a bad index?
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, a subclass of IndexOutOfBoundsException.

topics.name: Stack

beginner.content:
What is a Stack?

A stack is a pile where you only touch the top. The last item you put on is the first item you take off: LIFO (Last In, First Out). Think of a pile of plates, or the Back button of a browser: the page you visited most recently is the first one you go back to.

  • The class java.util.Stack extends Vector, so it is a growable array in which the end of the array is the top of the stack.
  • Only five methods are special: push, pop, peek, empty and search.
  • Because it extends Vector, it is synchronized (thread-safe, slower) and also exposes all Vector/List methods (get(i), add(i, e), ...), which can break the LIFO discipline.
  • Allows duplicates and null. Starts with capacity 10 and doubles when full.
  • Modern advice: the Java documentation itself recommends Deque<E> stack = new ArrayDeque<>() for new code. Learn Stack for interviews and to read old code.

Where Stack sits in the Collection Framework

Collection

(I)

The five Stack methods at a glance

MethodWhat it doesOn an empty stackTime
push(e)Puts e on top and returns it-O(1) amortised
pop()Removes and returns the top elementthrows EmptyStackExceptionO(1)
peek()Returns the top element without removing itthrows EmptyStackExceptionO(1)

search(o)Position of o counted from the top (1 = top), or -1-1O(n)

Your first Stack program

  • Items go on top with push; the printed list shows the bottom first and the top last.
  • pop takes the top item off, so the order of removal is the reverse of the order of adding.

intermediate.content:
The Stack methods

Each method with a runnable example.

push(E item)

  • Signature: E push(E item)
  • Returns: the item that was pushed
  • Time: O(1) amortised

For freshers: Puts the item on the top of the stack. It also returns the item, which is handy in expressions.

For experienced developers: Internally it calls addElement(item), so the "top" is the last index of the underlying array (the opposite of Deque.push, which adds at the front). The vector grows by doubling when it is full.

pop()

  • Signature: E pop()
  • Returns: the removed top element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Removes the top element and returns it. If the stack is empty it throws EmptyStackException, so check empty() first when the stack might be empty.

For experienced developers: Implemented as peek() then removeElementAt(size - 1): no shifting because the top is the last slot. EmptyStackException is an unchecked RuntimeException.

peek()

  • Signature: E peek()
  • Returns: the top element (not removed)
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Look at the top element without removing it. Use it to decide whether to pop. Throws EmptyStackException when empty.

For experienced developers: Unlike Deque.peek(), which returns null for an empty deque, Stack.peek() throws. Do not assume the two behave alike when you migrate.

empty()

  • Signature: boolean empty()
  • Returns: true if the stack has no elements
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Tells whether the stack is empty. It is the classic Stack name; isEmpty() (inherited from Vector) does exactly the same.

For experienced developers: The two names exist for historical reasons. Prefer isEmpty() in new code so the call works with any collection.

search(Object o)

  • Signature: int search(Object o)
  • Returns: the 1-based distance from the top, or -1
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Finds an element and tells how far it is from the top: the top element is at position 1, the next at 2, and so on. If the element is not there you get -1. If it appears several times, the one closest to the top is reported.

For experienced developers: It is size() - lastIndexOf(o). Note the two quirks: positions are 1-based and counted from the top, unlike indexOf which is 0-based from the bottom.

Inherited Vector methods

A Stack is a Vector, so every Vector method works. Be careful: the ones that touch the middle break the "only the top" rule.

Walking a Stack

  • Signature: for-each, iterator(), listIterator(), forEach(), stream(), get(i)
  • Returns: elements from the bottom to the top
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Iterating a Stack visits the elements from the bottom up (insertion order), which is the opposite of the order pop would return them. To print "top first" iterate backwards or use a ListIterator.

For experienced developers: This surprises people who switch to ArrayDeque or LinkedList used as a stack, where iteration goes from the top down. Do not rely on iteration order when you change the class.
codeExamples:
// Iterating a Stack goes bottom to top; popping goes top to bottom
import java.util.ArrayDeque;    // imports the ArrayDeque class
import java.util.Deque;         // imports the Deque class
import java.util.ListIterator;  // imports the ListIterator class
import java.util.Stack;         // imports the Stack class

public class StackIterationDemo {             // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {  // program entry point
        Stack<String> stack = new Stack<>();  // creates an empty Stack named stack
        stack.push("Raigad");                 // pushes "Raigad" on top of the stack
        stack.push("Sinhagad");               // pushes "Sinhagad" on top of the stack
        stack.push("Torna");                  // pushes "Torna" on top of the stack

        System.out.print("for-each (bottom to top): ");  // prints the text "for-each (bottom to top): "
        for (String fort : stack) {                      // loops over every element of stack
            System.out.print(fort + " ");                // prints the result
        }
        System.out.println();                            // prints an empty line

        System.out.print("top to bottom           : ");  // prints the text "top to bottom           : "
        ListIterator<String> it = stack.listIterator(stack.size());  // start at the end
        while (it.hasPrevious()) {                       // runs while there is an earlier element
            System.out.print(it.previous() + " ");       // prints the next element
        }
        System.out.println();                            // prints an empty line

        Deque<String> modern = new ArrayDeque<>();  // creates an empty ArrayDeque named modern
        modern.push("Raigad");                      // pushes "Raigad" on top of the stack
        modern.push("Sinhagad");                    // pushes "Sinhagad" on top of the stack
        modern.push("Torna");                       // pushes "Torna" on top of the stack
        System.out.println("ArrayDeque used as stack iterates top first: " + modern);  // prints a label followed by the value
    }
}
// OUTPUT:
// for-each (bottom to top): Raigad Sinhagad Torna
// top to bottom           : Torna Sinhagad Raigad
// ArrayDeque used as stack iterates top first: [Torna, Sinhagad, Raigad]

intermediate.content:
Methods that break the LIFO rule

  • Signature: get(i), add(i, e), remove(i), set(i, e), insertElementAt(e, i)
  • Returns: work on any position
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: Because Stack inherits the Vector (List) methods, nothing stops you from reading or removing in the middle. That is legal, but then it is no longer a true stack.

For experienced developers: This is a design flaw of java.util.Stack (inheritance instead of composition) and a main reason that Deque/ArrayDeque is recommended: it exposes only the end operations.

Stack as the modern Deque

  • Signature: Deque stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); push, pop, peek
  • Returns: LIFO with a clean API
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: The recommended replacement is ArrayDeque used through the Deque interface. It has the same push, pop and peek names but offers only end operations, is not synchronized (so faster) and returns null from peek() on an empty stack.

For experienced developers: Differences to remember: Deque.pop() throws NoSuchElementException (not EmptyStackException), peek() returns null, ArrayDeque forbids null elements, and iteration goes from the top down.

expert.content:
Where stacks are used

LIFO order appears all over programming. Four classic jobs, each with a program:

  • Matching brackets in a compiler or editor.
  • Reversing a sequence.
  • Undo / Back history in applications and browsers.
  • Evaluating expressions (postfix notation) and the call stack of method calls, including recursion.

Example 1: checking balanced brackets

Push every opening bracket; when a closing bracket arrives, the top of the stack must be its partner.

Example 2: reversing and the browser Back button

Pushing then popping reverses the order. A Back button keeps visited pages on a stack.

Example 3: evaluating a postfix expression

In postfix notation the operator comes after its operands: 6 2 3 + * means 6 * (2 + 3). A stack evaluates it in one pass.

Example 4: recursion is a stack

Every method call is pushed onto the JVM's call stack; returning pops it. Very deep recursion overflows that stack and throws StackOverflowError. You can replace recursion by your own Stack object.

Stack versus ArrayDeque versus LinkedList as a stack

StackArrayDequeLinkedList (as Deque)
Thread-safeYes (synchronized)NoNo
SpeedSlowest (locks)FastestFast, more memory
Allows nullYesNoYes
pop() on emptyEmptyStackExceptionNoSuchElementExceptionNoSuchElementException
peek() on emptyEmptyStackExceptionreturns nullreturns null
Iteration orderBottom to topTop to bottomTop to bottom
Exposes middle operationsYes (it is a Vector)NoYes (it is a List)
RecommendedLegacyYesOnly when you need List too

Best practices

Keep stacks correct and easy to maintain.

  • For new code use Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>().
  • Check empty() (or isEmpty()) before pop()/peek() unless an empty stack is a real bug.
  • Do not call get, add(i, e) or remove(i) on a stack; if you need them you want a List.
  • Replace deep recursion by an explicit stack when the depth can be large.
  • Declare the variable with the interface type (Deque) so you can change the class later.

interviewQA: What is a Stack and which principle does it follow?
A Stack is a LIFO structure: the last element pushed is the first one popped. In Java, java.util.Stack extends Vector and offers push, pop, peek, empty and search.
What is the difference between peek() and pop()?
Both return the top element; peek() leaves it on the stack, pop() removes it. Both throw EmptyStackException on an empty Stack.
What does search() return?
The 1-based position of the element counted from the top of the stack (top = 1), the closest occurrence if there are duplicates, or -1 if absent.
Why is java.util.Stack discouraged?
It extends Vector, so it is synchronized (slow) and exposes List methods that break LIFO. ArrayDeque used through Deque is faster, has a clean end-only API and is recommended by the Javadoc.
Which exception is thrown by pop() on an empty Stack?
EmptyStackException (unchecked). A Deque throws NoSuchElementException for pop() and returns null for peek().
In which order does a for-each loop visit a Stack?
From the bottom to the top (insertion order), the reverse of the pop order. An ArrayDeque used as a stack iterates top first.
How do you check for balanced brackets?
Push each opening bracket; on a closing bracket pop and verify it is the matching opener; at the end the stack must be empty.
What is the call stack?
The JVM keeps a stack of frames for method calls: calling a method pushes a frame and returning pops it. Too deep a recursion throws StackOverflowError.
Is Stack thread-safe?
Its individual methods are synchronized (inherited from Vector), but compound actions such as peek-then-pop are not atomic.
How do you get a stack's elements top first?
Iterate with a ListIterator from the end, or use ArrayDeque, whose iterator already starts at the top.

topics.name: HashSet

beginner.content:
What is a HashSet?

A HashSet is a collection that never holds the same element twice. Add "Raigad" a second time and nothing happens. It is built for speed: asking "is this fort in the set?" takes roughly the same tiny time whether the set holds ten forts or ten million.

  • Package java.util. Implements the Set interface (a Collection with no duplicates).
  • No index: a set has no get(i). You ask whether something is in it, add it, remove it, or loop over it.
  • No guaranteed order: elements come out in an order decided by their hash codes. It can look random and can change when the set grows. If you need an order use LinkedHashSet (insertion order) or TreeSet (sorted).
  • One null is allowed.
  • Fast: add, remove and contains are O(1) on average.
  • Not thread-safe. Internally a HashSet is a HashMap whose keys are your elements.
  • Your element class must implement equals() and hashCode() properly (String, Integer and records already do).

Where HashSet sits in the Collection Framework

Iterable
(I)
← extends
Collection
(I)
← extends
Set
(I)
← implements
AbstractSet
(c)
← extends
HashSet
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. HashSet also implements Cloneable and Serializable. Its subclass LinkedHashSet adds insertion order.

Creating a HashSet: four constructors

  • new HashSet<>(): empty, capacity 16, load factor 0.75.
  • new HashSet<>(int initialCapacity): empty with room for about that many buckets.
  • new HashSet<>(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor): control both numbers.
  • new HashSet<>(Collection c): a set holding the elements of another collection (duplicates are dropped).

Your first HashSet program

  • add returns true if the element was new and false if it was already there.
  • The printed order is decided by the hash codes, not by the order of adding.

All HashSet methods at a glance

n is the number of elements, m the size of the other collection.

MethodWhat it doesTime

intermediate.content:
Adding elements

A set decides for you whether an element is new. The return value of add tells you what happened.

add(E e)

  • Signature: boolean add(E e)
  • Returns: true if the element was new, false if it was already present
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Puts the element into the set only if it is not already there. Use the return value to detect duplicates, for example to find the first repeated value in a list.

For experienced developers: It calls map.put(e, PRESENT) on the internal HashMap. A duplicate is detected with hashCode() (to find the bucket) then equals() (to compare inside the bucket). The existing element is kept; the new equal one is discarded.

addAll(Collection c): union

  • Signature: boolean addAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the set changed
  • Time: O(m)

For freshers: Adds every element of another collection. Because a set ignores duplicates, addAll performs a union of two groups.

For experienced developers: It loops over c calling add. Pass a HashSet as the receiver and any collection as the argument; the result never contains duplicates.

Looking things up

The reason to use a HashSet: very fast membership tests.

contains(Object o) and containsAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o); boolean containsAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(1) / O(m)

For freshers: contains tells whether the element is in the set. It does not scan the whole set: it jumps straight to the right bucket. containsAll tests that every element of another collection is present (a "subset" test).

For experienced developers: Compare: ArrayList.contains is O(n). Turning a big list into a HashSet before many lookups is one of the most common performance fixes. Lookup cost degrades only when many elements share a bucket (bad hashCode).

size(), isEmpty() and clear()

  • Signature: int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: the count / whether empty / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(1) / O(capacity)

For freshers: Count the elements, test for none, or remove all of them.

For experienced developers: clear() empties the table but keeps its capacity, so the set does not shrink. Clearing a set that once held millions of elements leaves a big, empty table behind; create a new set if memory matters.

Removing elements

Remove one element, a group, the elements that match a rule, or everything outside a group.

remove(Object o)

  • Signature: boolean remove(Object o)
  • Returns: true if the element was present
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Removes the element if it is there and tells you whether it was. No shifting, because a set has no positions.

For experienced developers: It deletes the entry from the bucket. As with add, the lookup uses hashCode then equals.

removeAll, retainAll and removeIf

  • Signature: boolean removeAll(Collection c); boolean retainAll(Collection c); boolean removeIf(Predicate filter)
  • Returns: true if the set changed
  • Time: O(n) typical

For freshers: removeAll(c) is set difference (A minus B). retainAll(c) is intersection (what both sets share). removeIf removes everything that matches a rule written as a lambda.

For experienced developers: They are inherited from AbstractSet/Collection. For removeAll, Java chooses to iterate the smaller of the two collections when the argument is a Set, which keeps it fast. The argument's contains speed matters: pass a Set, not a List.

Walking and converting

A set has no index, so you visit every element with a loop, an iterator or a stream.

for-each, iterator() and forEach()

  • Signature: for (E e : set) ...; Iterator iterator(); void forEach(Consumer)
  • Returns: each element once, in hash order
  • Time: O(n + capacity)

For freshers: Visit every element. The order is not insertion order and is not guaranteed. Remove while walking only through Iterator.remove() (or removeIf), otherwise you get ConcurrentModificationException.

For experienced developers: The iterator walks the bucket array, so its cost is proportional to capacity + size; a mostly empty large table is slow to iterate. The iterator is fail-fast.

stream(), toArray() and clone()

  • Signature: Stream stream(); Object[] toArray(); Object clone()
  • Returns: a stream / an array / a shallow copy
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Process the elements with a stream pipeline, copy them into an array, or make a shallow copy of the set.

For experienced developers: The stream is unordered (the set has no order), so results of findFirst are arbitrary. Prefer the copy constructor new HashSet<>(set) to clone().

equals, hashCode, toString and Set.of

  • Signature: boolean equals(Object); int hashCode(); String toString(); Set.of(...) / Set.copyOf(...)
  • Returns: comparison / hash / text / immutable sets
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Two sets are equal when they hold the same elements, whatever the order or the Set class. Set.of(...) creates an immutable set (add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException, no nulls, no duplicates allowed at creation).

For experienced developers: Set.of rejects duplicate arguments with IllegalArgumentException, and its iteration order is randomised per JVM run (on purpose, to stop code depending on it).

Common jobs with a HashSet

Three everyday uses.

Remove duplicates from a list

Copy the list into a set. To keep the original order use LinkedHashSet instead of HashSet.
Union, intersection and difference of two groups

Fast lookups: a set instead of a list

The program counts how many blocked forts appear in a long list of visits, using a list lookup (O(n) each) and a set lookup (O(1) each). The counts are equal; only the work differs.

expert.content:
How HashSet works inside

A HashSet is a thin wrapper over a HashMap<E, Object>; every element is a key and every value is the same dummy object PRESENT.

  • Step 1, hash: h = e.hashCode(), then spread: h ^ (h >>> 16) so the high bits also influence the low bits.
  • Step 2, bucket: the table length is always a power of two, so the index is (n - 1) & hash, a fast "modulo".
  • Step 3, compare: inside the bucket Java compares hash codes first, then == / equals(). A match means "already present".
  • Collisions: elements that land in the same bucket form a linked list; if a bucket reaches 8 entries and the table has at least 64 buckets, the list is converted to a balanced red-black tree (O(log n) instead of O(n)).
  • Resize: when size > capacity * loadFactor (default 16 x 0.75 = 12) the table doubles and every entry is redistributed.
  • Capacity from the copy constructor: max(size / 0.75 + 1, 16), so copying avoids early resizes.
  • Because the order depends on hash codes and table size, iteration order can change after a resize.

Trap: equals() and hashCode() must agree

  • Rule: equal objects must have equal hash codes.
  • If a class overrides equals but not hashCode, two equal objects usually land in different buckets, so the set keeps both and contains fails.
  • A record (or an IDE-generated pair) gets both right.

Trap: changing an element after adding it

  • The bucket of an element is chosen from its hashCode when it is added.
  • If you later change a field that hashCode uses, the element sits in the wrong bucket: contains and remove can no longer find it.
  • Use immutable classes (records, Strings, Integers) as set elements.

Choosing a Set implementation

HashSetLinkedHashSetTreeSetCopyOnWriteArraySet
OrderNoneInsertion orderSorted (natural or Comparator)Insertion order
add / remove / containsO(1) averageO(1) averageO(log n)O(n)
InsideHashMapHashMap + linked listRed-black tree (TreeMap)Array copied on write
nullOne allowedOne allowedNot allowed (natural order)Allowed
Thread-safeNoNoNoYes
Use forDefault setPredictable iterationSorted data, range queriesFew writes, many readers

Best practices

Habits for fast and correct sets.

  • Declare with the interface: Set<String> forts = new HashSet<>();.
  • Give an expected size to avoid resizes: new HashSet<>((int) (expected / 0.75f) + 1) or HashSet.newHashSet(expected) (Java 19+).
  • Use immutable element types; always override equals and hashCode together (or use a record).
  • Do not depend on iteration order; use LinkedHashSet or TreeSet when you need one.
  • Prefer a Set over a List whenever you mostly ask "is it in there?" or must keep values unique.
  • To share between threads use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() or Collections.synchronizedSet.

Real example: tracking unique visitors of each fort

A visitor log with repeated entries. A set per fort counts each visitor once, and the intersection finds visitors who came to both.

interviewQA: What is a HashSet and how does it differ from an ArrayList?
HashSet stores unique elements with no order and no index, giving O(1) average add/remove/contains. ArrayList keeps insertion order, allows duplicates and has O(n) contains.
How does HashSet detect duplicates?
It computes the element hashCode, finds the bucket, and compares candidates with equals(). A match means the element is already present and add() returns false.
Is the iteration order of a HashSet guaranteed?
No. It depends on hash codes and the table size and may change after a resize. Use LinkedHashSet for insertion order or TreeSet for sorted order.
How is HashSet implemented internally?
As a HashMap whose keys are the elements and whose values are a shared dummy object (PRESENT).
What are load factor and initial capacity?

Capacity is the number of buckets (default 16); the load factor (default 0.75) is how full the table may get before it doubles and rehashes. A lower load factor means fewer collisions but more memory.
What happens on a hash collision?
Entries in the same bucket form a linked list; with 8 or more entries in a bucket and a table of at least 64 buckets the list becomes a red-black tree, improving the worst case from O(n) to O(log n).
Why must equals() and hashCode() be overridden together?
Equal objects must produce the same hash code, or they land in different buckets and the set treats them as different elements.
Why is mutating an element after adding it dangerous?
Its bucket was chosen from the old hash code. After the change contains() and remove() look in the wrong bucket and the element appears lost.
Does HashSet allow null?
Yes, one null element. TreeSet with natural ordering does not allow null.
How do you perform union, intersection and difference with sets?
Union: addAll; intersection: retainAll; difference: removeAll (on copies, because they modify the receiver).
HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet?
HashSet is fastest with no order; LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order at a small cost; TreeSet keeps elements sorted with O(log n) operations and supports range queries.
Is HashSet thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(), Collections.synchronizedSet(...) or CopyOnWriteArraySet depending on the access pattern.
How do you remove duplicates from a list while keeping order?
new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)).

topics.name: LinkedHashSet

beginner.content:
What is a LinkedHashSet?

A LinkedHashSet is a HashSet that remembers the order in which you added the elements. You still get no duplicates and fast lookups, but when you print or loop, the elements come out exactly in insertion order. Think of a visitor register: each fort is written once, in the order of the first visit.

  • Package java.util. It extends HashSet and, since Java 21, also implements SequencedSet.
  • No duplicates (the same rule as HashSet). Adding an element that is already present does not change its position.
  • Predictable order: iteration follows insertion order.
  • Fast: add, remove and contains are O(1) on average, with a small extra cost to maintain the order.
  • One null is allowed. Not thread-safe.
  • Use it when you need uniqueness and a stable order: removing duplicates from a list while keeping the order, caches, "recently seen" lists, report output.

Where LinkedHashSet sits in the Collection Framework

Collection
(I)
← extends
Set
(I)
← implements
HashSet
(c)
← extends
LinkedHashSet
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. LinkedHashSet inherits every HashSet method; it only changes how the elements are linked together inside.

Creating a LinkedHashSet

  • new LinkedHashSet<>(): empty, capacity 16, load factor 0.75.
  • new LinkedHashSet<>(int initialCapacity) and (int, float loadFactor): tune the size.
  • new LinkedHashSet<>(Collection c): a copy in the iteration order of c, duplicates dropped.

All LinkedHashSet methods at a glance

MethodWhat it doesTime
add(e) / addAll(c)Adds new elements at the end of the orderO(1) / O(m)
remove(o) / removeAll(c) / retainAll(c) / removeIf(p) / clear()Removes elements (the order of the rest stays)O(1) / O(n)
contains(o) / containsAll(c) / size() / isEmpty()Lookups and countsO(1)
iterator() / forEach(a) / stream() / toArray()Walk or convert in insertion orderO(n)
addFirst(e) / addLast(e)Adds at the front or end, moving an existing element (Java 21)O(1)
getFirst() / getLast()Reads the first / last element (Java 21)O(1)
removeFirst() / removeLast()Removes the first / last element (Java 21)O(1)
reversed()A reversed view (Java 21)O(1)
clone() / equals / hashCode / toStringCopy and compare (equality ignores order)O(n)

intermediate.content:
Adding, keeping the order and ignoring duplicates

LinkedHashSet behaves like HashSet, plus a stable order.

add(E e) and addAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean add(E e); boolean addAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if something was added
  • Time: O(1) / O(m)

For freshers: Adds an element at the end of the order if it is new. If it is already present nothing changes, and it keeps its old position (re-adding does not move it).

For experienced developers: Internally each entry is a LinkedHashMap.Entry with before and after links in addition to the HashMap bucket link. Insertion order is not affected by re-insertion; this is different from addFirst/addLast (Java 21) which do move.

contains, remove and the order of the rest

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o); boolean remove(Object o)
  • Returns: true / false
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Look up or remove an element by value, like a HashSet. After a removal the remaining elements keep their relative order.

For experienced developers: Removing unlinks the entry from both the bucket chain and the doubly linked order list, which is O(1) because it already has both neighbours.

removeAll, retainAll and clear

  • Signature: boolean removeAll(Collection c); boolean retainAll(Collection c); void clear()
  • Returns: true if changed / nothing
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Subtract a group, keep only a group, or remove everything. Unlike HashSet, the result keeps the insertion order of what is left, so printed results are the same every time.

For experienced developers: These are the same inherited methods as HashSet; the benefit of LinkedHashSet is the predictable output, which makes it very good for logs, reports and unit tests.

Walking and converting

Every way of visiting the elements follows the insertion order.

iterator, for-each, forEach, stream and toArray

  • Signature: Iterator iterator(); void forEach(Consumer); Stream stream(); Object[] toArray()
  • Returns: the elements in insertion order
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: All of them visit the elements in the order they were first added. Because the elements are also linked in a chain, iterating costs O(size), not O(capacity + size) as in HashSet.

For experienced developers: This makes LinkedHashSet faster to iterate than HashSet when the set is large but sparse. Streams over it are ordered streams.

Java 21: the first and the last element

Java 21 made LinkedHashSet a SequencedSet, which finally gives direct access to both ends.

getFirst, getLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed

  • Signature: E getFirst(); E getLast(); E removeFirst(); E removeLast(); SequencedSet reversed()
  • Returns: the element / a reversed view
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read or remove the first or last element without writing a loop. On an empty set they throw NoSuchElementException. reversed() gives a view that walks from the last element to the first.

For experienced developers: Before Java 21 you had to iterate to the end to find the last element. reversed() is a live view, not a copy.

addFirst(E) and addLast(E) (Java 21)

  • Signature: void addFirst(E e); void addLast(E e)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Add an element at the front or the end. If the element is already in the set it is moved to that position. This is the first way to re-order a LinkedHashSet without rebuilding it.

For experienced developers: This is different from add, which never moves an existing element. It makes LinkedHashSet usable as a simple "move to front" structure.

clone, equals, hashCode and toString

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); int hashCode(); String toString()
  • Returns: copy / comparison / hash / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: clone makes a shallow copy that keeps the order. equals follows the Set rule: same elements means equal, and order is ignored. toString prints the elements in insertion order.

For experienced developers: Even though it is ordered, LinkedHashSet.equals does not compare the order (a List would). Two sets with the same elements in different order are equal and have the same hash code.

expert.content:
How LinkedHashSet works inside

LinkedHashSet is a HashSet whose internal map is a LinkedHashMap.

  • The constructor calls super(capacity, loadFactor, true), a package-private HashSet constructor that creates a LinkedHashMap instead of a plain HashMap.
  • Each entry carries before and after references. The map keeps head (eldest) and tail (youngest) so iteration just follows after pointers.
  • Lookups still go through the hash table, so contains/add/remove are O(1) like HashSet.
  • Memory: two extra references (8 bytes with compressed pointers) per element on top of the HashMap entry.
  • Iteration is O(size) because it ignores empty buckets (HashSet iteration is O(capacity + size)).
  • The "access order" mode (for LRU caches) exists only on LinkedHashMap, not on LinkedHashSet.

HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet side by side

HashSetLinkedHashSetTreeSet
OrderNoneInsertion orderSorted
add / remove / containsO(1)O(1)O(log n)
IterationO(capacity + n)O(n)O(n)
MemoryLowestA bit moreMost (tree nodes)
nullOneOneNo
Use forPlain uniquenessUniqueness + stable orderSorted data

Trap: you cannot sort a LinkedHashSet or index into it

  • A set has no get(i) and no sort. To sort, copy into a TreeSet or a List.
  • To get an element by position, copy to a list: new ArrayList<>(set).get(i).

Best practices

When and how to use LinkedHashSet well.

  • Choose it when you need uniqueness and a predictable order, for example to remove duplicates from a list without reordering.
  • Prefer plain HashSet when order does not matter: it uses less memory.
  • Use immutable elements and consistent equals/hashCode, as for any hash-based collection.
  • Use getFirst/getLast/reversed (Java 21) instead of iterating to find the ends.
  • For an LRU cache use LinkedHashMap with access order, not a set.

Real example: a "recently visited" list without repeats

Each visit moves a fort to the end of the list; the set never holds a fort twice, and the oldest visit is easy to drop.

interviewQA: What is a LinkedHashSet?
A HashSet that also keeps a doubly linked list through its entries, so it stores unique elements and iterates them in insertion order, with O(1) add/remove/contains.
Difference between HashSet and LinkedHashSet?
HashSet has no defined order and uses less memory; LinkedHashSet iterates in insertion order and has two extra references per entry. Both are O(1) for add, remove and contains.
How is LinkedHashSet implemented?
It extends HashSet and constructs a LinkedHashMap as the backing map; each entry has before/after links, and the map keeps head and tail.
What happens if you add an element that already exists?
The set is unchanged and the element keeps its original position (plain add never moves it). With Java 21 addFirst/addLast do move an existing element.
Does equals() on a LinkedHashSet consider order?
No. Two sets with the same elements are equal regardless of order.
How do you remove duplicates from a list and keep the order?
new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)).
Why is iteration over LinkedHashSet faster than HashSet for sparse tables?
LinkedHashSet follows the chain of entries (O(size)), while HashSet iterates over all buckets (O(capacity + size)).
What did Java 21 add to LinkedHashSet?
The SequencedSet methods: getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed.
Does LinkedHashSet allow null?
Yes, one null element, like HashSet.
Is LinkedHashSet thread-safe?
No. Wrap with Collections.synchronizedSet or use a concurrent structure.

topics.name: TreeSet

beginner.content:
What is a TreeSet?

A TreeSet is a set that keeps its elements sorted at all times. Add forts in any order and they come out alphabetically; add numbers and they come out from small to large. It also never holds duplicates, and it can answer questions such as "which fort comes right after Raigad?" or "give me all forts between P and S".

  • Package java.util. Implements NavigableSet (which extends SortedSet, which extends Set).
  • Sorted order: by the elements' natural order (Comparable) or by a Comparator you supply.
  • No duplicates: "duplicate" means compareTo / compare returns 0, not equals().
  • Slower than HashSet: add, remove and contains are O(log n) because it is a balanced tree.
  • No null with natural ordering (it cannot compare null). Not thread-safe.
  • Elements must be mutually comparable, otherwise ClassCastException.
  • Use it when you need sorted output or range and neighbour queries.

Where TreeSet sits in the Collection Framework

(I) = interface, (c) = class. TreeSet extends AbstractSet and is built on a TreeMap.

Creating a TreeSet: four constructors

  • new TreeSet<>(): natural ordering of the elements.
  • new TreeSet<>(Comparator c): your own ordering.
  • new TreeSet<>(Collection c): copy with natural ordering, duplicates dropped.
  • new TreeSet<>(SortedSet s): copy that keeps the ordering of s.

All TreeSet methods at a glance

intermediate.content:
Adding and the sorted order

Whatever order you add in, the elements are kept sorted.

add(E e) and addAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean add(E e); boolean addAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the element was new
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Inserts the element at the position that keeps the set sorted. If an element that compares as equal (compareTo returns 0) is already present, nothing is added.

For experienced developers: The tree walks from the root comparing with compareTo (or the comparator), so the cost is the height of the tree: O(log n). Because uniqueness is decided by the comparison, a comparator that ignores a field also treats elements that differ in that field as duplicates (see the trap below).

remove, contains, size, isEmpty and clear

  • Signature: boolean remove(Object o); boolean contains(Object o); int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: true / false / count
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Remove and look up by value, count the elements, or remove all. The set stays sorted after every change.

For experienced developers: Lookups use the same comparison as add, so they need a comparable argument; contains(null) throws NullPointerException with natural ordering.

The ends: first, last, pollFirst and pollLast

Because the set is sorted, the smallest and the largest elements are always easy to reach.

first() and last()

  • Signature: E first(); E last()
  • Returns: the smallest / the largest element
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Return the smallest and the largest element without removing them. On an empty set they throw NoSuchElementException.

For experienced developers: In Java 21, getFirst() and getLast() are the equivalent sequenced-collection names. Both walk down the left-most or right-most branch of the tree.

pollFirst() and pollLast()

  • Signature: E pollFirst(); E pollLast()
  • Returns: the removed element, or null if empty
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Remove and return the smallest or the largest element. Use them to treat a TreeSet like a priority queue that has no duplicates: repeat pollFirst until it returns null.

For experienced developers: Safe for empty sets (they return null), unlike removeFirst in Java 21 which throws. Because a TreeSet cannot contain null, a null result is unambiguous here.

Neighbours: lower, floor, ceiling and higher

The reason people choose a TreeSet over a HashSet. Given a value, find the closest elements even if the value itself is not in the set.

lower, floor, ceiling and higher

  • Signature: E lower(E e); E floor(E e); E ceiling(E e); E higher(E e)
  • Returns: the neighbour, or null if there is none
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Four "nearest element" questions: lower(e) = the greatest element strictly below e; floor(e) = the greatest element below or equal; ceiling(e) = the smallest element above or equal; higher(e) = the smallest element strictly above. Memory trick: floor and lower look down; ceiling and higher look up; floor/ceiling may return e itself.

For experienced developers: Each is one root-to-leaf walk. They are what make TreeSet useful for "find the next time slot", "nearest price", "which range does this value fall in". e does not have to be in the set.

Range views: headSet, tailSet and subSet

Take a part of the set by value. The result is a live view of the same data.

headSet, tailSet and subSet

  • Signature: SortedSet headSet(E to); NavigableSet headSet(E to, boolean inclusive); tailSet(from[, inclusive]); subSet(from, to) / subSet(from, fromInc, to, toInc)
  • Returns: a view of that range
  • Time: O(log n) to create

For freshers: headSet(to) = everything before to; tailSet(from) = everything from from onwards; subSet(from, to) = from (included) up to to (excluded). The longer forms let you choose whether each end is included.

For experienced developers: These are views, not copies: changing the view changes the set and vice versa, and adding an element outside the range to the view throws IllegalArgumentException. Wrap in new TreeSet<>(view) for an independent copy.

Reverse order and iteration

Walk the set from the end, or look at it upside down.

descendingSet(), descendingIterator() and reversed()

  • Signature: NavigableSet descendingSet(); Iterator descendingIterator(); NavigableSet reversed()
  • Returns: a reversed view / iterator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: descendingSet() shows the same elements from largest to smallest, as a live view. descendingIterator() walks them that way. In Java 21 reversed() does the same as descendingSet().

For experienced developers: Views are free (no copying). Because it is a NavigableSet itself, you can chain operations, for example set.descendingSet().headSet(x).

iterator, forEach, stream and comparator()

  • Signature: Iterator iterator(); void forEach(Consumer); Stream stream(); Comparator comparator()
  • Returns: elements in sorted order / the ordering in use
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Iteration, forEach and streams all visit the elements in sorted order. comparator() returns the Comparator that defines the order, or null when natural ordering is used.

For experienced developers: Streams from a TreeSet are SORTED and DISTINCT, so stream().sorted() is free and distinct() is redundant. The iterator is fail-fast.

expert.content:
How TreeSet works inside

A TreeSet is a thin wrapper over a TreeMap<E, Object> (the values are the shared PRESENT object). The TreeMap is a red-black tree.

  • A binary search tree keeps smaller elements in the left subtree and larger ones in the right subtree, so a lookup discards half of the remaining elements at each step.
  • A plain BST can degrade into a list when you add sorted data. The red-black rules (each node red or black, no two red nodes in a row, equal black height on every path) are restored by rotations and recolouring after each insert or delete, so the height never exceeds about 2 log2(n+1).
  • That guarantees O(log n) for add, remove, contains, floor, ceiling, first and last. One million elements need about 20 comparisons.
  • Every node stores key, value, left, right, parent and a colour flag: roughly 40 bytes per element, more than HashSet.
  • Order is defined only by compareTo / compare. equals() and hashCode() are never used.
  • Iteration walks the tree in order via successor links: O(1) amortised per step.

Natural ordering: elements must be Comparable

  • Strings, Integers, Doubles, Dates and enums are already Comparable.
  • For your own class, implement Comparable<T> (one natural order) or pass a Comparator (any order).
  • Adding a class that is not comparable throws ClassCastException on the first add.

Trap: the comparator decides what a "duplicate" is

  • A TreeSet treats two elements as the same when the comparison returns 0.
  • If your comparator looks only at the length of a name, "Torna" and "Lohag" (both length 5) are "equal", and the second is silently not added.
  • Always add a tie-breaker (thenComparing) so the comparator is consistent with equals unless you really want to merge such elements.

Real use: finding the nearest slot with ceiling and floor

A tour operator has fixed departure hours. For a requested hour, ceiling gives the next departure and floor the previous one: an O(log n) query a HashSet cannot answer.

TreeSet versus HashSet versus LinkedHashSet versus ConcurrentSkipListSet

TreeSetHashSetLinkedHashSetConcurrentSkipListSet
OrderSortedNoneInsertionSorted
add / remove / containsO(log n)O(1)O(1)O(log n)
Neighbour / range queriesYesNoNoYes
nullNoOneOneNo
Thread-safeNoNoNoYes (lock-free)
Uniqueness decided bycompareTo / Comparatorequals / hashCodeequals / hashCodecompareTo / Comparator

Best practices

Use TreeSet when order matters, and use it carefully.

  • Choose TreeSet only when you need sorted iteration or neighbour/range queries; otherwise HashSet is faster.
  • Keep the comparator consistent with equals and never throw from it; always add a tie-breaker.
  • Use immutable elements, or at least never change a field that takes part in the comparison after adding (the element would sit in the wrong place in the tree).
  • Do not add null; guard inputs.
  • Declare as NavigableSet / SortedSet when you use their methods, or Set when you do not.
  • For concurrent use choose ConcurrentSkipListSet.

interviewQA: What is a TreeSet and when would you use it?
A TreeSet is a sorted NavigableSet backed by a red-black tree (a TreeMap). Use it when you need unique elements in sorted order or neighbour/range queries (floor, ceiling, headSet, tailSet).
Time complexity of TreeSet operations?
add, remove, contains, first, last, floor, ceiling, higher and lower are O(log n); iteration is O(n) in sorted order.
How does TreeSet decide whether two elements are duplicates?
By compareTo (natural ordering) or the Comparator returning 0, not by equals() or hashCode().
Can a TreeSet contain null?
Not with natural ordering: comparing null throws NullPointerException. A custom comparator could accept null, but that is rare and discouraged.
What happens if the elements are not Comparable?
ClassCastException is thrown on the first add unless you supply a Comparator.
Difference between floor, lower, ceiling and higher?
lower: greatest strictly less; floor: greatest less than or equal; ceiling: smallest greater than or equal; higher: smallest strictly greater. Each returns null if no such element exists.
What are headSet, tailSet and subSet?
Live range views: headSet(to) is the elements before to, tailSet(from) from from onwards, subSet(from, to) from from (inclusive) to to (exclusive). The long forms allow choosing inclusivity.
HashSet vs TreeSet?
HashSet: unordered, O(1), one null, equals/hashCode. TreeSet: sorted, O(log n), no null, compareTo/Comparator, supports navigation and ranges.
How is TreeSet implemented?
It wraps a TreeMap, a self-balancing red-black tree where each element is a key and the value is a dummy object.
Why is a comparator that is inconsistent with equals dangerous in a TreeSet?
Elements the comparator considers equal are treated as duplicates and the later ones are silently dropped, even if equals() says they differ.
Is TreeSet thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentSkipListSet or Collections.synchronizedSortedSet.
How do you get a descending view?
descendingSet() (or reversed() in Java 21) returns a live reversed view; descendingIterator() returns a reverse iterator.

topics.name: HashMap

beginner.content:
What is a HashMap?

A HashMap stores pairs: a key and the value that belongs to it. You give the map a key and it gives back the value almost instantly, like looking up a city in a telephone-code table: key "Pune", value 20. Each key appears once; each key maps to one value.

  • Package java.util. Implements Map<K, V>. It is not a Collection (it has its own interface).
  • Unique keys: putting an existing key again replaces the value. Values may repeat.
  • Fast: get, put, remove and containsKey are O(1) on average.
  • No order: iteration order depends on hash codes and can change when the map grows. Use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap for an order.
  • One null key and any number of null values are allowed.
  • Not thread-safe. For threads use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Key classes must have correct equals() and hashCode() (String, Integer and records already do).

Where HashMap sits in the Collection Framework

Map
(I)
← implements
AbstractMap
(c)
← extends
HashMap
(c)
← extended by
LinkedHashMap
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. HashMap also implements Cloneable and Serializable. Its subclass LinkedHashMap adds a predictable order.

Creating a HashMap: four constructors

  • new HashMap<>(): empty, capacity 16, load factor 0.75.
  • new HashMap<>(int initialCapacity) and (int, float loadFactor): tune the table size.
  • new HashMap<>(Map m): a copy of another map.
  • Declare the variable as Map<K, V>, not HashMap.

Your first HashMap program

  • put(key, value) adds a pair; get(key) returns the value or null if the key is missing.
  • Printing a map shows {key=value, key=value}.
  • Putting the same key again replaces the value and returns the old one.

All HashMap methods at a glance

n is the number of entries.

MethodWhat it doesTime

get(k) / getOrDefault(k, d)Reads a value (null / default when missing)O(1)
containsKey(k) / containsValue(v)Tests for a key / for a valueO(1) / O(n)

replace(k, v) / replaceAll(f)Replaces one value / transforms every valueO(1) / O(n)

intermediate.content:
Putting pairs in

Four ways to add: replace freely, add a whole map, add only when missing, or compute.

put(K key, V value)

  • Signature: V put(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the previous value for the key, or null if there was none
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Stores the pair. If the key is new the pair is added and null is returned. If the key exists, its value is replaced and the old value is returned.

For experienced developers: The key's hashCode selects a bucket; the key is then compared with equals inside the bucket. On a replace the original key object is kept, only the value changes. A null return is ambiguous when null values are allowed (use containsKey to tell).

putAll(Map m)

  • Signature: void putAll(Map m)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(m)

For freshers: Copies every pair of another map into this one. Keys that already exist get their value replaced.

For experienced developers: It pre-sizes the table for the incoming entries and then does one put per entry. Use it to merge two maps: the argument "wins" on conflicts.

putIfAbsent(K key, V value)

  • Signature: V putIfAbsent(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the existing value, or null if the pair was added
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Adds the pair only if the key has no value yet. If the key is already there nothing changes and you get the existing value back. It is the safe way to write "set a default".

For experienced developers: It is one atomic call instead of if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) (two lookups, and a race in concurrent code). A key mapped to null counts as "no value" and is filled.

Reading values

Read by key. A missing key gives null, unless you ask for a default.

get(Object key) and getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)

  • Signature: V get(Object key); V getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)
  • Returns: the value, or null / the default if the key is missing
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: get returns the value stored for the key, or null when the key is absent. getOrDefault lets you give a value to use instead of null, which avoids a NullPointerException when you unbox the result.

For experienced developers: A null from get can mean "no key" or "the value is null". Use containsKey to tell them apart. int hours = map.get("x") throws NullPointerException when the key is missing because of the unboxing; getOrDefault("x", 0) does not.

containsKey(Object key) and containsValue(Object value)

  • Signature: boolean containsKey(Object key); boolean containsValue(Object value)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: containsKey asks "is this key in the map?" and is very fast. containsValue asks "does any key have this value?" and has to scan every entry, so it is slow on big maps.

For experienced developers: If you need fast "by value" lookups, keep a second map from value to key, or use a bidirectional map from a library. containsKey also tells you whether get returned null because of a missing key or a null value.

size(), isEmpty() and clear()

  • Signature: int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: the count / emptiness / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(1) / O(capacity)

For freshers: Count the pairs, test for none, or remove every pair.

For experienced developers: clear() removes the entries but keeps the table size, so a map that once held millions of entries stays big in memory. Create a new map if you want to release it.

Removing and replacing

Remove by key, remove conditionally, and replace without adding new keys.

remove(Object key) and remove(Object key, Object value)

  • Signature: V remove(Object key); boolean remove(Object key, Object value)
  • Returns: the removed value (or null) / true if removed
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: remove(key) deletes the pair and returns the value that was stored. remove(key, value) deletes it only if the key currently has exactly that value.

For experienced developers: The two-argument form is a compare-and-remove, useful for "remove this entry only if nobody changed it".

replace(K, V) and replaceAll(BiFunction)

  • Signature: V replace(K key, V value); boolean replace(K key, V oldValue, V newValue); void replaceAll(BiFunction function)
  • Returns: the old value / whether replaced / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: replace(key, value) changes the value only if the key exists (unlike put, it never adds a new key). replaceAll(function) recalculates every value from its key and old value.

For experienced developers: replaceAll is a clean way to transform all values in place, for example "add 1 to every count" or "make all values upper case".

Calculating values: compute, computeIfAbsent, computeIfPresent and merge

These four methods (Java 8) replace the old "get, check, put" pattern. They do the lookup once.

computeIfAbsent(K, Function)

  • Signature: V computeIfAbsent(K key, Function mappingFunction)
  • Returns: the existing or newly computed value
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: If the key has no value, call the function to create one, store it and return it. If the key already has a value, return it and do not call the function. The classic use is a map of lists: map.computeIfAbsent(city, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(fort).

For experienced developers: The function must not modify the map (it can throw ConcurrentModificationException). Returning null from the function means "do not store anything".

computeIfPresent(K, BiFunction)

  • Signature: V computeIfPresent(K key, BiFunction remappingFunction)
  • Returns: the new value, or null if removed / absent
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: If the key exists (with a non-null value), call the function with the key and the old value and store the result. If the function returns null the entry is removed. If the key is missing nothing happens.

For experienced developers: Perfect for "update if it exists" and for "decrement, and delete when it reaches zero".

compute(K, BiFunction)

  • Signature: V compute(K key, BiFunction remappingFunction)
  • Returns: the new value (or null if the entry was removed)
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: Calls the function whether or not the key exists. The function receives the key and the old value (or null) and returns the new value. A null result removes the entry. Use it for a counter: map.compute(word, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1).

For experienced developers: Compared with merge, compute sees the key and can treat "absent" and "present" differently in one expression.

merge(K, V, BiFunction)

  • Signature: V merge(K key, V value, BiFunction remappingFunction)
  • Returns: the new value in the map
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: The shortest way to count or to combine values. If the key is absent, it stores the given value. If the key is present, it stores function(oldValue, givenValue). A null result removes the entry. Counting words: map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum).

For experienced developers: The function takes the two values (not the key), so method references such as Integer::sum, String::concat or Math::max fit perfectly. Neither the value nor the function may be null.

Walking through a map

A map offers three views: the keys, the values and the pairs. Choose the one that gives you what you need in a single loop.

keySet(), values() and entrySet()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet()
  • Returns: live views
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: keySet() is the set of keys, values() the collection of values and entrySet() the set of key-value pairs (Map.Entry). They are views: removing from a view removes from the map. Loop over entrySet() when you need both key and value; looping over keySet() and calling get does an extra lookup for every key.

For experienced developers: Views do not support add. The iteration order is the map's order (for HashMap: arbitrary). Removing during iteration must go through the iterator, removeIf on the view, or Map.removeIf-style calls on entrySet().

forEach(BiConsumer)

  • Signature: void forEach(BiConsumer action)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n + capacity)

For freshers: Runs an action for every pair, written as a lambda with two parameters: map.forEach((key, value) -> ...). It is the shortest loop when you only need to read.

For experienced developers: Cannot break out of it. It is fail-fast: changing the map inside the lambda throws ConcurrentModificationException at the end of the loop.

Iterating safely: removing while looping

  • Signature: entrySet().iterator() with remove(), entrySet().removeIf(...), keySet().removeIf(...)
  • Returns: removes pairs without an exception
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Removing from a map inside a for-each loop throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use an Iterator, or the one-line entrySet().removeIf(...).

For experienced developers: This is the same fail-fast rule as for lists. HashMap checks a modification counter on each step.

Copies, equality and immutable maps

Finish with the helper methods.

clone, equals, hashCode and toString

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); int hashCode(); String toString()
  • Returns: a shallow copy / comparison / hash / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Two maps are equal when they have the same keys with equal values, whatever the Map class and the order. clone() makes a shallow copy (keys and values are shared).

For experienced developers: Prefer new HashMap<>(map) to clone(). The map's hash code is the sum of the hash codes of its entries, so it is order-independent.

Map.of, Map.entry, Map.ofEntries and Map.copyOf

  • Signature: Map.of(k1, v1, ...); Map.entry(k, v); Map.ofEntries(...); Map.copyOf(map)
  • Returns: an immutable map / entry
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Create small immutable maps quickly. Map.of takes up to 10 key-value pairs; Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(...), ...) takes any number; Map.copyOf makes an immutable copy. They reject null and duplicate keys, and any change throws UnsupportedOperationException.

For experienced developers: Their iteration order is deliberately randomised per JVM run. Wrap with new HashMap<>(Map.of(...)) when you need a modifiable map, as in the other examples of this page.

expert.content:
How HashMap works inside

Everything in the tables above follows from a few ideas.

  • Storage: an array of buckets, Node<K,V>[] table, whose length is always a power of two (default 16). Each Node holds hash, key, value and next.
  • Hash: h = key.hashCode(), then h ^ (h >>> 16) to mix the high bits into the low bits. A null key always hashes to 0 (bucket 0).
  • Index: index = (n - 1) & hash, which is a fast way of writing hash % n for a power-of-two n.
  • put: if the bucket is empty the node goes in. Otherwise Java compares each node: same hash and (same reference or equals) means "same key, replace value"; if no node matches, the new node is appended to the bucket's chain.
  • Treeify: when a chain reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the chain becomes a red-black tree (O(log n) lookup in a crowded bucket). With fewer buckets, the table is resized instead. A tree shrinks back to a list at 6 nodes.
  • Resize: when size > threshold (capacity x loadFactor = 12 for the default), the table doubles and nodes are redistributed. Because the size doubles, each node either stays at its index or moves by exactly the old capacity.
  • Lazy: the table is created on the first put. new HashMap<>(n) rounds n up to a power of two (tableSizeFor).
  • Iteration cost is O(capacity + size) because it scans all buckets.
  • Not thread-safe: concurrent resizes can lose entries (and in old JDKs loop forever). Use ConcurrentHashMap.

Time complexity summary

OperationAverageWorst caseNote
get, put, remove, containsKeyO(1)O(log n) (O(n) before Java 8)Worst case when many keys share one bucket
containsValueO(n)O(n)Scans every entry

Trap: keys need equals() and hashCode(); never mutate a key

  • A key without hashCode/equals is compared by identity, so a "new equal" key does not find the value.
  • If you change a field used by hashCode after the key is in the map, the entry sits in the wrong bucket and can no longer be found.
  • Immutable keys (String, Integer, enums, records) avoid both problems.

Real example 1: word frequency

The most common HashMap job: count how often each item appears, then show the result sorted.

Real example 2: a lookup cache

Store the result of a slow calculation so the second request for the same key is instant. computeIfAbsent runs the calculation only once per key.

Best practices

Habits for correct and fast maps.

  • Declare as Map<K, V>.
  • Use immutable keys and always override equals and hashCode together (or use a record).
  • Use getOrDefault, merge, computeIfAbsent and putIfAbsent instead of "get, check, put".
  • Iterate with entrySet() (or forEach) when you need both key and value.
  • Pre-size big maps: HashMap.newHashMap(expected) (Java 19+) or new HashMap<>((int) (expected / 0.75f) + 1).
  • Do not rely on iteration order; choose LinkedHashMap or TreeMap when you need one.
  • Use ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps, not HashMap and not Hashtable.
  • Do not use a mutable collection as a key.

interviewQA: How does HashMap work internally?

It keeps an array of buckets (power-of-two size). The key hash is spread (h ^ h>>>16), the bucket index is (n-1)&hash, and entries in the same bucket form a linked list that becomes a red-black tree when it reaches 8 nodes (table >= 64). When size exceeds capacity x load factor the table doubles.
What is the default capacity and load factor?
16 buckets and 0.75, so the first resize happens when the 13th entry is added.
What happens when two keys have the same hash code?
They go to the same bucket; equals() decides whether they are the same key (replace value) or different keys (both stored in the chain/tree).
What does put() return?
The previous value for the key, or null if the key was new (or its value was null).
Why must equals() and hashCode() be overridden together for keys?
HashMap finds the bucket with hashCode and the entry with equals. If equal keys can have different hash codes, lookups look in the wrong bucket and fail.
Can HashMap have null keys or values?
One null key (stored in bucket 0) and any number of null values. Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap allow neither.
HashMap vs Hashtable?
HashMap is unsynchronized, allows one null key and null values, and is faster; Hashtable is a legacy synchronized class that allows no nulls. Use ConcurrentHashMap for thread safety.
HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap?
HashMap: no order, O(1). LinkedHashMap: insertion or access order, O(1). TreeMap: sorted by key, O(log n), supports navigation.
What is the difference between getOrDefault and putIfAbsent?
getOrDefault only reads and returns the default without storing it; putIfAbsent stores the value when the key has none.
How do you count occurrences with a HashMap?
map.merge(item, 1, Integer::sum) (or compute with a null check).
How do you iterate a HashMap?
entrySet() with for-each (best when you need keys and values), keySet(), values(), or forEach((k, v) -> ...).
Why does HashMap throw ConcurrentModificationException?
Its iterators are fail-fast: they compare modCount with the value seen at creation, so structural changes during iteration (other than through the iterator) are detected.
How can HashMap lose data in multi-threaded code?
Concurrent puts and resizes can overwrite each other or corrupt the table. Use ConcurrentHashMap or external synchronization.
What is treeification?
When a bucket holds 8 or more nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the linked list is replaced by a red-black tree to keep worst-case lookups at O(log n).
Which is faster for a mostly-read lookup of a million entries: HashMap or TreeMap?
HashMap (O(1) average versus O(log n)), unless you need sorted order or range queries.

topics.name: LinkedHashMap

beginner.content:
What is a LinkedHashMap?

A LinkedHashMap is a HashMap that remembers the order of its entries. Everything you know about HashMap still applies (unique keys, O(1) lookups, one null key), but when you print or loop over it, the pairs come out in a predictable order: the order in which the keys were first added.

  • Package java.util. It extends HashMap and (Java 21) implements SequencedMap.
  • Insertion order (default): iteration follows the order of first insertion. Putting an existing key again does not move it.
  • Access order (optional): with the constructor flag accessOrder = true the most recently read or written entry moves to the end. This is the basis of an LRU cache.
  • Fast: get, put and remove are O(1) on average, with a small extra cost to keep the links.
  • One null key and null values are allowed. Not thread-safe.
  • Use it for: reports and JSON output in a stable order, "last seen" lists, LRU caches.

Where LinkedHashMap sits in the Collection Framework

(I) = interface, (c) = class. In Java 21 SequencedMap was added between Map and LinkedHashMap/TreeMap.

Creating a LinkedHashMap

  • new LinkedHashMap<>(): empty, insertion order.
  • new LinkedHashMap<>(int initialCapacity) and (int, float loadFactor): tune the table.
  • new LinkedHashMap<>(int, float, boolean accessOrder): true means access order.
  • new LinkedHashMap<>(Map m): a copy in the iteration order of m.

All LinkedHashMap methods at a glance
