intermediate.content:
Insertion order in action

All the HashMap methods work; the new thing is the order of every view and loop.

put, get, remove and the order of pairs

  • Signature: V put(K, V); V get(Object); V remove(Object)
  • Returns: as HashMap
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: New keys are added at the end of the order. Putting a key that already exists replaces its value but keeps its position. Removing a key just closes the gap.

For experienced developers: Each entry is a LinkedHashMap.Entry with before and after links in addition to the bucket link, so adding, removing and reordering are all O(1) pointer changes.

keySet(), values(), entrySet() and forEach()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet(); void forEach(BiConsumer)
  • Returns: views in insertion order
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Every view and every loop visits the pairs in insertion order, so printed results are the same on every run: ideal for reports, logs and tests.

For experienced developers: Iteration costs O(size), not O(capacity + size), because it follows the entry chain and skips empty buckets.

computeIfAbsent, merge and the other compute methods

  • Signature: compute / computeIfAbsent / computeIfPresent / merge
  • Returns: as HashMap
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: They behave exactly as in HashMap. A new key created by one of them is added at the end of the order.

For experienced developers: When you build a grouped or counted result that you later print, LinkedHashMap gives you the groups in the order they were first seen.

Access order and the LRU cache

The special power of LinkedHashMap.

Access order: new LinkedHashMap(capacity, loadFactor, true)

  • Signature: LinkedHashMap(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor, boolean accessOrder)
  • Returns: a map ordered by last access
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: With accessOrder = true, every get or put of a key moves that entry to the end. So the first entry is always the least recently used one and the last entry is the most recently used.

For experienced developers: In access-order mode even get is a structural modification (it re-links the entry), so iterating while calling get throws ConcurrentModificationException. containsKey, containsValue and the views do not count as access.

removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest)

  • Signature: protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest)
  • Returns: true to remove the eldest entry after an insertion
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: LinkedHashMap calls this method after every put. By default it returns false. Override it to return true when the map is too big and the oldest entry is removed automatically. Together with access order this builds an LRU (least recently used) cache in a few lines.

For experienced developers: The method may also modify the map itself, but the usual pattern is just return size() > MAX. Wrap the class with Collections.synchronizedMap for thread safety (or use Caffeine for a production cache).

Java 21: first and last entries

The new SequencedMap methods.

firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry and pollLastEntry

  • Signature: Map.Entry firstEntry(); lastEntry(); pollFirstEntry(); pollLastEntry()
  • Returns: the entry, or null if the map is empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read or remove the first or last pair directly. The poll versions remove and return it. The returned entries are snapshots (immutable).

For experienced developers: Before Java 21 you had to iterate to the end to find the last entry. With pollFirstEntry in a loop a LinkedHashMap can act as an ordered work queue with key lookups.

putFirst, putLast and reversed

  • Signature: V putFirst(K, V); V putLast(K, V); SequencedMap reversed()
  • Returns: the previous value / a reversed view
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: putFirst and putLast add a pair at the front or the back; if the key already exists it is moved there. reversed() is a live view that walks from the last entry to the first.

For experienced developers: This finally allows reordering a LinkedHashMap without removing and re-adding. sequencedKeySet(), sequencedValues() and sequencedEntrySet() give the same ordered views with getFirst, getLast and reversed.

clone, equals and toString

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString()
  • Returns: a shallow copy / comparison / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A LinkedHashMap is equal to any other Map with the same pairs; the order is ignored by equals. toString prints the pairs in order.

For experienced developers: Copy with new LinkedHashMap<>(map) to keep the order of the source map.

expert.content:
How LinkedHashMap works inside

It adds one doubly linked list on top of HashMap's buckets.

  • Entries are LinkedHashMap.Entry<K,V>: a HashMap node plus before and after references. The map keeps head (eldest) and tail (youngest).
  • HashMap exposes three hooks that LinkedHashMap overrides: afterNodeInsertion (calls removeEldestEntry), afterNodeAccess (moves the entry to the tail in access-order mode) and afterNodeRemoval (unlinks the entry).
  • Lookups still use the hash table, so get, put and remove stay O(1).
  • Iteration follows after links: O(size), independent of capacity.
  • Memory: two extra references (8 bytes with compressed pointers) per entry compared with HashMap.
  • In access-order mode get relinks the entry, so it changes modCount and is not safe for concurrent readers.

Trap: get() changes the order in access-order mode

  • A read relinks the entry, so reading while iterating the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Iterate over a copy of the keys (or entries) when you need to read inside the loop.

Real example: ordered JSON-style report

Fields must appear in the order they were defined, so a LinkedHashMap is the natural container for a record that will be written out.

Best practices

When LinkedHashMap is the right tool.

  • Use it when the order of iteration matters (output, serialization, tests) and you still want O(1) lookups.
  • For caches use access order plus removeEldestEntry, but wrap it for threads (Collections.synchronizedMap) or use a library cache.
  • Do not read the map inside a loop over the same map in access-order mode.
  • Use plain HashMap when order does not matter: it needs less memory.
  • Use immutable keys with consistent equals/hashCode, as for any hash map.
  • In Java 21 prefer firstEntry, lastEntry, putFirst, putLast and reversed() to hand-written iteration.

interviewQA: What is a LinkedHashMap and how does it differ from HashMap?

It is a HashMap that also keeps a doubly linked list through its entries, so iteration follows insertion order (or access order) instead of hash order. Operations stay O(1) with slightly more memory per entry.
How do you create an LRU cache in Java?
Extend LinkedHashMap, call super(capacity, 0.75f, true) for access order, and override removeEldestEntry to return size() > capacity.
What is access order?
A mode enabled by the third constructor argument: each get or put moves the entry to the end, so the first entry is the least recently used.
What does removeEldestEntry do?
It is called after each insertion with the eldest entry; returning true removes it. The default returns false.
Does re-inserting an existing key change its position?
Not in insertion-order mode. In access-order mode it moves to the end. In Java 21, putFirst/putLast move it explicitly.
Is LinkedHashMap thread-safe?
No. In access-order mode even get() modifies the structure. Use Collections.synchronizedMap or a concurrent cache.
Why is iteration over LinkedHashMap faster than HashMap for sparse tables?
It follows the entry chain (O(size)) instead of scanning all buckets (O(capacity + size)).
What did Java 21 add to LinkedHashMap?
SequencedMap methods: firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry, putFirst, putLast, reversed and sequenced views of keys, values and entries.
Does equals() of a LinkedHashMap consider order?
No. Two maps with the same pairs are equal regardless of order.
When would you choose TreeMap over LinkedHashMap?
When you need entries sorted by key or navigation methods (floorKey, headMap, ...). LinkedHashMap orders by insertion/access, not by key.

topics.name: TreeMap

beginner.content:
What is a TreeMap?

A TreeMap is a map whose keys are always kept sorted. Put the pairs in any order and they come out ordered by key: forts A to Z, numbers small to large. On top of the ordinary map methods it can answer neighbour and range questions: "which key comes just after 500?" or "give me all entries between P and S".

  • Package java.util. Implements NavigableMap (which extends SortedMap, which extends Map).
  • Sorted by key: by the keys' natural order (Comparable) or by a Comparator you supply.
  • Unique keys: two keys are "the same" when compareTo / compare returns 0 (not when equals says so).
  • O(log n) for get, put, remove and containsKey: slower than HashMap but ordered.
  • No null key with natural ordering; null values are allowed.
  • Not thread-safe. Use ConcurrentSkipListMap for concurrent sorted maps.
  • Use it for: sorted output, range queries, "nearest" lookups, rate tables and time lines.

  • new TreeMap<>(Comparator c): your own key ordering.
  • new TreeMap<>(Map m): copy with natural ordering.
  • new TreeMap<>(SortedMap m): copy that keeps the ordering of m.

intermediate.content:
Putting and reading: the sorted map

All the usual Map methods work, and every view is in key order.

put, get, remove and containsKey

  • Signature: V put(K, V); V get(Object); V remove(Object); boolean containsKey(Object)
  • Returns: as Map
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Same meaning as in HashMap, but the map keeps itself sorted. A new key is inserted at its sorted place; an existing key just has its value replaced.

For experienced developers: Each call walks from the root comparing the key, so the cost is the tree height. Passing a key that is not comparable throws ClassCastException; passing null throws NullPointerException (natural ordering).

merge, computeIfAbsent and the other compute methods

  • Signature: compute / computeIfAbsent / computeIfPresent / merge / putIfAbsent / getOrDefault
  • Returns: as HashMap
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: They behave exactly as in HashMap. Combine them with a TreeMap to get sorted counts and groups.

For experienced developers: A TreeMap is often the finishing step of a data pipeline: collect into a HashMap for speed, then copy into a TreeMap to print in order.

keySet(), values(), entrySet() and forEach()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet(); void forEach(BiConsumer)
  • Returns: views in ascending key order
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Every view and loop is in ascending key order. They are live views: removing from a view removes from the map.

For experienced developers: navigableKeySet() returns the keys as a NavigableSet and descendingKeySet() in reverse. Entries from entrySet() support setValue, but entries returned by firstEntry() and friends are immutable snapshots.

The ends of the map

Smallest and largest key, with or without removing them.

firstKey, lastKey, firstEntry and lastEntry

  • Signature: K firstKey(); K lastKey(); Map.Entry firstEntry(); Map.Entry lastEntry()
  • Returns: the key / the entry
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: firstKey() and lastKey() return the smallest and the largest key and throw NoSuchElementException when the map is empty. firstEntry() and lastEntry() return the whole pair (or null when empty).

For experienced developers: The entry versions are safer for possibly-empty maps and give the value in the same call. The returned entries are snapshots: calling setValue on them throws UnsupportedOperationException.

pollFirstEntry() and pollLastEntry()

  • Signature: Map.Entry pollFirstEntry(); Map.Entry pollLastEntry()
  • Returns: the removed entry, or null if empty
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Remove and return the entry with the smallest or the largest key. Repeat pollFirstEntry until it returns null to process entries in key order while consuming them (a sorted queue with lookups).

For experienced developers: Handy for event schedulers: key = time, value = task; pollFirstEntry always gives the next task due.

Neighbours: lowerKey, floorKey, ceilingKey and higherKey

Find the closest key to a value, even if the value is not a key. Each has an Entry twin: lowerEntry, floorEntry, ceilingEntry, higherEntry.

lowerKey, floorKey, ceilingKey, higherKey (and the Entry versions)

  • Signature: K lowerKey(K); K floorKey(K); K ceilingKey(K); K higherKey(K); Map.Entry lowerEntry(K) ...
  • Returns: the neighbouring key / entry, or null
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: lowerKey(k) = greatest key strictly below k; floorKey(k) = greatest key below or equal; ceilingKey(k) = smallest key above or equal; higherKey(k) = smallest key strictly above. If there is no such key the result is null.

For experienced developers: The Entry versions return the key and its value in one call, which is what you usually want. This is the standard way to implement price slabs, tax brackets, grade boundaries and time-line lookups.

Range views: headMap, tailMap and subMap

Take a part of the map by key. The result is a live view.

headMap, tailMap and subMap

  • Signature: SortedMap headMap(K toKey); NavigableMap headMap(K toKey, boolean inclusive); tailMap(K fromKey[, boolean]); subMap(from, to) / subMap(from, fromInc, to, toInc)
  • Returns: a view of that key range
  • Time: O(log n) to create

For freshers: headMap(to) = entries with keys before to; tailMap(from) = keys from from onwards; subMap(from, to) = from (included) to to (excluded). The long forms let you choose whether each end is included.

For experienced developers: Views are not copies: changing the view changes the map and the other way round. Putting a key outside the view's range throws IllegalArgumentException. Copy with new TreeMap<>(view) for an independent map.

Reverse order

See the map upside down without copying it.

descendingMap(), descendingKeySet(), navigableKeySet() and reversed()

  • Signature: NavigableMap descendingMap(); NavigableSet descendingKeySet(); NavigableSet navigableKeySet(); NavigableMap reversed()
  • Returns: live reversed / key-set views
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: descendingMap() shows the same entries from the largest key to the smallest. descendingKeySet() does the same for the keys only. In Java 21 reversed() is the same as descendingMap().

For experienced developers: All are views: they update when the map changes, and removing through them changes the map. They can be chained: map.descendingMap().headMap(x).

comparator(), clone, equals and toString

  • Signature: Comparator comparator(); Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString()
  • Returns: the ordering / a shallow copy / comparison / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: comparator() returns the ordering in use (null for natural ordering). A TreeMap is equal to any Map with the same pairs, whatever the order or class.

For experienced developers: A clone copies the structure and keeps the comparator. Because equals on maps uses equals of the keys, a TreeMap with an unusual comparator can be "not equal" to a HashMap that looks identical.

expert.content:
How TreeMap works inside

TreeMap is a red-black tree: a binary search tree that rebalances itself.

  • Every node (TreeMap.Entry) stores key, value, left, right, parent and a colour flag (red or black).
  • The binary-search-tree rule: all keys in the left subtree are smaller, all keys in the right subtree are larger. A lookup therefore discards half of the remaining keys at every step.
  • The red-black rules (root is black; a red node has black children; every path from a node to its leaves has the same number of black nodes) are repaired after each insert/delete by rotations and recolouring. The height stays at most about 2 log2(n + 1).
  • So get, put, remove, floorKey, ceilingKey, firstKey ... are all O(log n): about 20 comparisons for a million entries.
  • Ordering comes only from compareTo or the Comparator. hashCode is never used; equals is not used to find keys.
  • Iteration walks the tree in order using successor links: O(1) amortised per step, O(n) overall.
  • Memory: about 40 bytes of overhead per entry (more than HashMap).

Trap: the comparator decides which keys are "the same"

  • If the comparator returns 0 for two different keys, the second put replaces the value of the first key and no new entry is created.
  • Add tie-breakers with thenComparing so that only truly equal keys compare as 0.

Real example 1: tax / price slabs with floorEntry

A table of slabs keyed by the lower bound. floorEntry(amount) finds the slab that contains any amount in one O(log n) call.

Real example 2: an event timeline with subMap

Keep events keyed by hour; subMap returns everything in a time window.

TreeMap versus HashMap versus LinkedHashMap versus ConcurrentSkipListMap

TreeMapHashMapLinkedHashMapConcurrentSkipListMap
OrderSorted by keyNoneInsertion / accessSorted by key
get / put / removeO(log n)O(1)O(1)O(log n)
Range / neighbour queriesYesNoNoYes
null keyNoOneOneNo
Thread-safeNoNoNoYes (lock-free)
Key identity decided bycompareTo / Comparatorequals / hashCodeequals / hashCodecompareTo / Comparator

Best practices

Use TreeMap for what only it can do.

  • Choose TreeMap when you need sorted keys, "nearest key" lookups or range queries; otherwise HashMap is faster.
  • Keep the comparator consistent with equals and add tie-breakers (thenComparing).
  • Never modify a key in a way that changes its ordering after inserting it.
  • Do not use null keys. Check inputs.
  • Prefer the *Entry navigation methods to the *Key ones when you also need the value.
  • For a concurrent sorted map use ConcurrentSkipListMap; for a one-off sorted print, copy a HashMap into a TreeMap.

interviewQA: What is a TreeMap and how is it implemented?
A sorted NavigableMap implemented as a red-black tree: a self-balancing binary search tree that keeps keys ordered and guarantees O(log n) get, put, remove and navigation.
Time complexity of TreeMap operations?
get, put, remove, containsKey, floorKey, ceilingKey, firstKey, lastKey: O(log n). Iteration is O(n) in key order; containsValue is O(n).
How does TreeMap decide whether two keys are equal?
With compareTo or the Comparator returning 0; equals() and hashCode() are not used.
Can TreeMap have null keys or values?
No null keys with natural ordering (NullPointerException); null values are allowed.
What happens when keys are not Comparable?
ClassCastException when you put the first key, unless you pass a Comparator.
Explain floorKey, ceilingKey, lowerKey and higherKey.

lowerKey: greatest key strictly less; floorKey: greatest key <=; ceilingKey: smallest key >=; higherKey: smallest key strictly greater. They return null if no such key exists. The *Entry versions return the entry.
What do headMap, tailMap and subMap return?
Live range views: headMap(to) keys before to, tailMap(from) keys from from onwards, subMap(from, to) from inclusive to exclusive; overloads allow inclusivity flags.
HashMap vs TreeMap?
HashMap: unordered, O(1), one null key, equals/hashCode. TreeMap: sorted by key, O(log n), no null keys, compareTo/Comparator, navigation and range views.
How do you sort a HashMap by key and by value?
By key: new TreeMap<>(hashMap). By value: put the entries in a list and sort it with Map.Entry.comparingByValue(), or stream entrySet().sorted(...) into a LinkedHashMap.
Is TreeMap thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentSkipListMap or Collections.synchronizedSortedMap.
What is a consistent-with-equals comparator and why does it matter?
It returns 0 only when equals() is true. Otherwise a TreeMap treats keys that equals() says are different as the same key and replaces values.
How do you get entries in descending key order?
descendingMap() (or reversed() in Java 21), or construct the TreeMap with Comparator.reverseOrder().

topics.name: Hashtable

beginner.content:
What is a Hashtable?

Hashtable is the original (Java 1.0) key-value store. It works like a HashMap but every method is synchronized, and it refuses null keys and values. Today it is a legacy class: you will meet it in old code and interviews, but new code should use HashMap (single thread) or ConcurrentHashMap (many threads).

  • Package java.util. Extends the old Dictionary class and implements Map.
  • Thread-safe: each method locks the whole table, so only one thread works at a time.
  • No null key and no null value: put(null, x) and put(k, null) throw NullPointerException.
  • No guaranteed order, and it iterates in a different order from HashMap.
  • Default capacity 11, load factor 0.75, grows to 2 * old + 1.
  • Index = (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length. Buckets are plain linked lists (no tree conversion).
  • Legacy extras: keys(), elements() (Enumeration) and contains().

Where Hashtable sits in the Collection Framework

Hashtable
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. Properties extends Hashtable and is used for configuration files.

Creating a Hashtable: four constructors

  • new Hashtable<>(): capacity 11, load factor 0.75.
  • new Hashtable<>(int capacity): chosen start size.
  • new Hashtable<>(int capacity, float loadFactor): both chosen.
  • new Hashtable<>(Map m): copy of another map.

All Hashtable methods at a glance

Every method is synchronized.

get(k)Value for a key, or null if absentO(1) average

intermediate.content:
Adding and reading

The basic methods, with the null rules that set Hashtable apart.

put(K key, V value)

  • Signature: V put(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the old value, or null for a new key
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Stores the pair. Putting an existing key replaces its value and returns the old one. Neither the key nor the value may be null.

For experienced developers: It locks the whole table. The key must implement hashCode and equals correctly. A null key fails at key.hashCode(); a null value is explicitly rejected.

get(Object key), getOrDefault and containsKey

  • Signature: V get(Object key); V getOrDefault(Object key, V default); boolean containsKey(Object key)
  • Returns: the value / default / boolean
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: get returns the value for a key or null when it is absent. Because values can never be null, null always means "no such key": a small advantage over HashMap.

For experienced developers: getOrDefault avoids the null check. get(null) throws NullPointerException.

remove(Object key), size(), isEmpty() and clear()

  • Signature: V remove(Object key); boolean remove(Object key, Object value); int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: old value / boolean / count
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: remove(key) deletes a pair and returns the old value (or null). The two-argument form deletes only when the value also matches. clear() empties the table.

For experienced developers: After clear() the internal array keeps its size; only the entries go.

containsValue(Object) and contains(Object)

  • Signature: boolean containsValue(Object value); boolean contains(Object value)
  • Returns: boolean
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Both ask "does any pair have this value?". contains is the legacy name and does exactly the same as containsValue.

For experienced developers: It scans every bucket, so it is slow on big tables. Beware: contains checks values, not keys, which surprises people used to Collection.contains.

Java 8 methods

The same atomic helpers as HashMap, and in Hashtable each one is also synchronized.

putIfAbsent, replace, merge and computeIfAbsent

  • Signature: V putIfAbsent(K, V); V replace(K, V); V merge(K, V, BiFunction); V computeIfAbsent(K, Function)
  • Returns: the previous / new value
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: putIfAbsent adds only a missing key; replace changes only an existing key; merge combines the old and new value (word counts, totals); computeIfAbsent builds a value only when the key is absent.

For experienced developers: In a Hashtable each of these runs under the table lock, so the check-and-act sequence is atomic. That is a real benefit, but ConcurrentHashMap gives the same safety with far less blocking.

Looping

Three ways: the modern views, forEach, and the legacy Enumeration.

keySet(), values(), entrySet() and forEach()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet(); void forEach(BiConsumer)
  • Returns: live views
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Loop over the keys, the values, or the pairs. The views are live: removing through them removes from the table.

For experienced developers: The order is not insertion order and not the same as a HashMap's. These iterators are fail-fast (as in HashMap), so changing the table inside a for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException.

keys() and elements() (legacy Enumeration)

  • Signature: Enumeration keys(); Enumeration elements()
  • Returns: an Enumeration
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: The Java 1.0 way to loop. An Enumeration has just hasMoreElements() and nextElement(). You will see it in old code.

For experienced developers: Unlike an Iterator, an Enumeration has no remove() and is not fail-fast. Prefer keySet() and entrySet() in new code.

putAll(Map), clone, equals and toString

  • Signature: void putAll(Map); Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString()
  • Returns: copy / comparison / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: putAll copies all pairs from another map, clone makes a shallow copy, equals compares the pairs, toString prints {k=v, ...}.

For experienced developers: A clone copies the table but shares the key and value objects. Two maps are equal when they hold the same pairs, whatever their class.

expert.content:
How Hashtable works inside

The structure is the one HashMap started from.

  • An array of Entry nodes; each bucket is a singly linked list (never converted to a tree, unlike HashMap since Java 8).
  • Bucket index = (key.hashCode() & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length. The modulo works on any size, so the default is the prime-ish number 11, not a power of two.
  • Rehash when count >= threshold (capacity x 0.75): new length = old * 2 + 1, and every entry is re-linked.
  • New entries are inserted at the head of the bucket list.
  • Locking: every public method is synchronized on the table itself. Reads block writes and other reads, so a busy table becomes a bottleneck.
  • Because hashCode() is called on the key without a null check, a null key throws NPE.

Trap: a synchronized table is not a synchronized program

  • Each method is atomic, but a check-then-act sequence made of two methods is not: another thread can slip in between containsKey and put.
  • Use the atomic methods (putIfAbsent, merge, computeIfAbsent) or hold your own lock around the whole sequence.

Real example: loading configuration with Properties

Properties extends Hashtable and holds String to String settings, with a default value for missing keys.

Hashtable versus HashMap versus ConcurrentHashMap versus synchronizedMap

Thread-safeYes (whole-table lock)NoYes (fine-grained / lock-free reads)Yes (one lock)
null keyNoOneNoDepends on the wrapped map
null valueNoYesNoDepends on the wrapped map
Speed (many threads)SlowFastest (single thread)FastSlow
Bucket structureLinked listList then treeList then treeAs wrapped
Default capacity111616As wrapped
StatusLegacyCurrentCurrentCurrent

Best practices

Know Hashtable, but do not choose it for new code.

  • Single thread: HashMap. Many threads: ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Keep Hashtable only when an old API forces it (for example Properties or an older library).
  • Never rely on a particular iteration order.
  • Do not combine containsKey and put to "add if missing": use putIfAbsent.
  • Do not modify a table while looping over it (fail-fast).

interviewQA: What is a Hashtable?
A legacy (Java 1.0) synchronized hash-based Map. It allows no null keys or values and has no guaranteed order.
Difference between HashMap and Hashtable?

Hashtable is synchronized (slow), forbids null keys and values, is legacy and extends Dictionary; HashMap is not synchronized, allows one null key and many null values, is faster and uses tree bins for long collision chains.
Why does Hashtable not allow null?
A null key fails on key.hashCode(); a null value is rejected so that get() returning null can only mean "key absent", which is safe to use in multi-threaded code.
Is Hashtable thread-safe? Is that enough?
Each method is, but compound actions such as containsKey then put are not atomic. Use putIfAbsent / merge / computeIfAbsent or external locking.
What is the default capacity and growth of Hashtable?
Capacity 11, load factor 0.75, new capacity = old * 2 + 1.
How is the bucket index computed?
(hashCode & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length. HashMap instead spreads the hash and uses (n - 1) & hash on a power-of-two table.
Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap?
ConcurrentHashMap locks only parts of the table (CAS and per-bin locks), reads are non-blocking and it scales; Hashtable locks the whole table for every call.
What is the difference between Enumeration and Iterator?
Enumeration is the legacy read-only cursor without remove() and without fail-fast behaviour; Iterator can remove and is fail-fast.
What is Properties?
A subclass of Hashtable for String to String settings, with getProperty(key, default), and load/store for .properties files.
Is Hashtable ordered?
No. Use LinkedHashMap for insertion order or TreeMap for sorted order.
How do you make a HashMap thread-safe?
Use ConcurrentHashMap (preferred) or wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap.

topics.name: Comparable Interface

beginner.content:
What is Comparable?

Comparable gives a class its natural order: the one default way two objects of that class are compared. It has a single method, compareTo. Once a class implements it, Collections.sort, Arrays.sort, TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue and stream().sorted() all know how to order it.

  • Package java.lang (no import needed). The interface is Comparable<T>.
  • One method: int compareTo(T other), implemented inside the class being sorted.
  • Return negative if this object comes first, zero if equal in order, positive if this comes later.
  • String, Integer, Long, Double, Character, LocalDate, BigDecimal and enums are already Comparable.
  • There can be only one natural order per class. For other orders use Comparator.

Where Comparable sits

Comparable<T>
(I)
← implements
String / Integer / LocalDate ...
(c)
← implements
Your class (Fort)
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. It is not part of the Collection hierarchy but sorted collections depend on it.

The contract in one picture

compareTo returnsMeaningExample

Zerosame position in the order"Torna".compareTo("Torna") is 0
Positivethis comes after other"Torna".compareTo("Raigad") is positive

intermediate.content:
Making your own class Comparable

Implement Comparable<YourClass> and write compareTo.

compareTo(T other)

  • Signature: int compareTo(T other)
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive int
  • Time: depends on your code

For freshers: Compare the field you want to sort by. Use the helper methods Integer.compare, Double.compare, String.compareTo instead of subtracting.

For experienced developers: Never write return this.x - other.x: the subtraction can overflow for large or negative values and give the wrong sign. Integer.compare(this.x, other.x) is always correct.

Sorting with the natural order

  • Signature: Collections.sort(list); Arrays.sort(array); list.sort(null); stream.sorted()
  • Returns: sorted in place / a sorted stream
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Every sorting tool uses compareTo when you do not give a Comparator. If the class is not Comparable you get a ClassCastException at run time.

For experienced developers: list.sort(null) means "use the natural order". The sort is stable for objects: equal elements keep their relative order.

Sorted collections: TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(); new TreeMap<>(); new PriorityQueue<>()
  • Returns: sorted containers
  • Time: O(log n) per add

For freshers: These containers keep elements ordered as you add them, using compareTo. A TreeSet of Comparable forts therefore prints in order and rejects duplicates.

For experienced developers: Here compareTo also decides duplicates: a TreeSet treats two objects as the same when compareTo returns 0, even if equals says they differ.

Choosing the field

The natural order is your decision: name, number, date. Pick the one that is most obviously "the" order.

Comparing by a number: descending and ascending

  • Signature: Integer.compare(a, b); Double.compare(a, b); Long.compare(a, b)
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: For ascending order write Integer.compare(this.x, other.x). For descending swap the arguments: Integer.compare(other.x, this.x).

For experienced developers: A natural order should be obvious. If readers could argue about whether "natural" means height or name, keep the natural order simple and use a Comparator for the rest.

Comparing by two fields (tie-breaker)

  • Signature: if (first != 0) return first; return second
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: When the first field is equal, compare a second one. This keeps the order total and avoids accidental duplicates in a TreeSet.

For experienced developers: Write the tie-break by hand as below, or build it with Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) and call it from compareTo.

expert.content:
Rules of a correct compareTo

Sorting algorithms assume these rules. Breaking them gives wrong order or IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract.

  • Antisymmetry: sign(a.compareTo(b)) == -sign(b.compareTo(a)).
  • Transitivity: if a < b and b < c then a < c.
  • Consistency: if a.compareTo(b) == 0 then a and b compare the same way against every other object.
  • Consistent with equals (strongly recommended): a.compareTo(b) == 0 exactly when a.equals(b). Otherwise TreeSet / TreeMap and HashSet / HashMap disagree about duplicates.
  • compareTo(null) should throw NullPointerException.
  • Never compare floating-point with - or by casting; use Double.compare (it also orders NaN and -0.0 correctly).

Trap: inconsistent with equals

A class that sorts by one field but defines equals on another behaves differently in a TreeSet and a HashSet.
Trap: subtraction overflows

Real example: a sorted fort register

A record can implement Comparable too, so a few lines give a fully ordered value type.

Comparable versus Comparator

ComparableComparator
Packagejava.langjava.util
MethodcompareTo(T other) (one object)compare(T a, T b) (two objects)
Where writtenInside the class being sortedOutside, in its own class / lambda
How many ordersOne (the natural order)As many as you like
Can sort classes you cannot editNoYes
Used by defaultsort(), TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueueOnly when you pass it in

Best practices

Keep the natural order simple and correct.

  • Implement Comparable only when one order is clearly "the" order (name, id, date).
  • Always use Integer.compare / Double.compare, never subtraction.
  • Keep compareTo consistent with equals and hashCode.
  • Compare the same fields in equals and compareTo; add a tie-breaker field if needed.
  • Use Comparator for any extra orders and for classes you cannot modify.
  • Do not use mutable fields in compareTo for objects stored in a TreeSet or TreeMap.

interviewQA: What is the Comparable interface?
A java.lang interface with one method, compareTo, that defines the natural ordering of a class; sorted collections and sort methods use it by default.
What does compareTo return?
Negative if this is less than the argument, zero if equal in order, positive if greater.
Comparable vs Comparator?
Comparable is implemented inside the class (one natural order, compareTo(T)); Comparator is a separate object (many orders, compare(T, T)) and works on classes you cannot edit.
What happens if a class is not Comparable and you put it in a TreeSet?
ClassCastException at run time when the first element is added (unless a Comparator was supplied).
Why not use subtraction in compareTo?
It can overflow and return the wrong sign. Use Integer.compare / Double.compare.
What does "consistent with equals" mean?
compareTo returns 0 exactly when equals returns true. If not, TreeSet/TreeMap and HashSet/HashMap treat duplicates differently.
Which built-in classes are Comparable?
String, the wrapper classes (Integer, Long, Double, Character...), BigInteger, BigDecimal, LocalDate/LocalDateTime, enums (by ordinal) and more.
How do you sort in descending order using Comparable?
Swap the operands in compareTo, or leave the natural order and sort with Collections.reverseOrder() / a reversed Comparator.
Can a class have more than one natural order?
No: compareTo gives exactly one. Use Comparators for other orders.
Is Collections.sort stable?
Yes for objects (it uses TimSort): equal elements keep their original relative order.

topics.name: Comparator Interface

beginner.content:
What is a Comparator?

A Comparator is a small object that says how to order two objects, kept outside the class. Use it when a class has no natural order, when you cannot edit the class, or when you need several different orders (by name, by height, by trek time...).

  • Package java.util. The interface is Comparator<T>.
  • The one abstract method: int compare(T a, T b) (negative: a first, zero: equal, positive: b first). Because there is only one, a Comparator can be written as a lambda.
  • Many ready-made helper methods (comparing, thenComparing, reversed, naturalOrder, nullsFirst...) build comparators in one line.
  • Pass it to list.sort(c), Collections.sort(list, c), Arrays.sort(a, c), new TreeSet<>(c), new TreeMap<>(c), new PriorityQueue<>(c) and stream.sorted(c).

Where Comparator sits

Comparator<T>
(I)
← implemented by
Lambda / method reference
(c)
← returned by
Comparator.comparing(...) results
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. Comparator is a @FunctionalInterface.

Your first Comparator: three ways to write the same thing

  • Anonymous class: the long, classic form.
  • Lambda: (a, b) -> a.name().compareTo(b.name()).
  • Helper method: Comparator.comparing(Fort::name): shortest and clearest.

All Comparator methods at a glance

MethodWhat it does
compare(a, b)The one abstract method: orders two objects
Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor)Order by a field (any Comparable)
comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator)Order by a field with your own comparator for it
comparingInt / comparingLong / comparingDoubleOrder by a primitive field, no boxing
thenComparing(...)Tie-breaker when the first order says equal
thenComparingInt / Long / DoubleTie-breaker on a primitive field
reversed()The opposite order
Comparator.naturalOrder() / reverseOrder()compareTo order / its opposite
Comparator.nullsFirst(c) / nullsLast(c)Handle null elements safely
Collections.reverseOrder()Reverse of the natural order (older style)
equals(obj)Inherited; rarely used

intermediate.content:
Building comparators with comparing()

Name the field and let Java do the comparing.

Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor)

  • Signature: static <T, U extends Comparable> Comparator<T> comparing(Function<T, U> keyExtractor)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Pass a method reference to the field you want to sort by. The result orders objects by that field using its natural order (strings A to Z, numbers small to large).

For experienced developers: The key must be Comparable. For an int field prefer comparingInt (no boxing).

comparingInt, comparingLong and comparingDouble

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparingInt(ToIntFunction<T>); comparingLong(...); comparingDouble(...)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Same as comparing but for int, long and double fields, without boxing every value into an object. Use them for numbers.

For experienced developers: Numbers sort ascending by default: smallest first. Add .reversed() for largest first.

reversed()

  • Signature: default Comparator<T> reversed()
  • Returns: the opposite Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Turns any comparator around: ascending becomes descending. Call it on a ready comparator.

For experienced developers: With a lambda comparator, Java may not infer the type, so write Comparator.comparingInt(Fort::heightMetres).reversed() (works) rather than starting from an untyped lambda.

thenComparing(...) and thenComparingInt(...)

  • Signature: default Comparator<T> thenComparing(Comparator / Function); thenComparingInt(ToIntFunction)
  • Returns: a Comparator with a tie-breaker
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Sort by one field first, then break ties with another: district, then name. Chain as many as you need.

For experienced developers: The later comparators are used only when all earlier ones return 0. Add .reversed() after a single step to reverse just that step, not the whole chain.

comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator)

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparing(Function<T, U> key, Comparator<U> keyComparator)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Compare by a field using your own rule for that field, for example case-insensitive text or reverse order.

For experienced developers: String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER is a ready comparator for text that ignores upper and lower case.

naturalOrder(), reverseOrder() and Collections.reverseOrder()

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> naturalOrder(); static Comparator<T> reverseOrder(); Collections.reverseOrder()
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: naturalOrder() uses compareTo; reverseOrder() is its opposite. They are handy for TreeSet, PriorityQueue and sorting lists of strings or numbers.

For experienced developers: Collections.reverseOrder() does the same as Comparator.reverseOrder() (the older way). Collections.reverseOrder(c) reverses any comparator.
codeExamples:
// naturalOrder / reverseOrder with lists, TreeSet and PriorityQueue
import java.util.ArrayList;      // imports the ArrayList class
import java.util.Collections;    // imports the Collections class
import java.util.Comparator;     // imports the Comparator class
import java.util.List;           // imports the List class
import java.util.PriorityQueue;  // imports the PriorityQueue class
import java.util.TreeSet;        // imports the TreeSet class

public class ComparatorNaturalReverseDemo {         // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {        // program entry point
        List<Integer> altitudes = new ArrayList<>(List.of(800, 100, 1200, 400));  // creates an ArrayList filled with the listed values
        altitudes.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());  // sorts using the given comparator
        System.out.println("List, high to low : " + altitudes);  // prints a label followed by the value

        TreeSet<String> cities = new TreeSet<>(Collections.reverseOrder());  // creates a TreeSet named cities copied from Collections.reverseOrder()
        cities.addAll(List.of("Pune", "Nagpur", "Mumbai"));   // adds every element of List.of("Pune", "Nagpur", "Mumbai... to the set
        System.out.println("TreeSet, Z to A   : " + cities);  // prints a label followed by the value

        PriorityQueue<Integer> queue = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());  // max-heap
        queue.addAll(List.of(5, 9, 2));  // adds every element of List.of(5, 9, 2) to the queue
        System.out.println("Max-heap poll     : " + queue.poll());  // prints the removed element
    }
}
// OUTPUT:
// List, high to low : [1200, 800, 400, 100]
// TreeSet, Z to A   : [Pune, Nagpur, Mumbai]
// Max-heap poll     : 9

intermediate.content:
nullsFirst(c) and nullsLast(c)

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> nullsFirst(Comparator<T>); static Comparator<T> nullsLast(Comparator<T>)
  • Returns: a null-safe Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Normal comparators throw NullPointerException on a null element or key. These wrappers place the nulls at the start or at the end and use your comparator for the rest.

For experienced developers: Use them whenever a sort key can be missing (an optional district, an unset date).

Where comparators are used

The same comparator works everywhere ordering is needed.

Sorted containers and streams

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(c); new TreeMap<>(c); new PriorityQueue<>(c); stream.sorted(c); Collections.max(list, c)
  • Returns: ordered containers / sorted stream
  • Time: O(log n) per add, O(n log n) to sort

For freshers: Hand the comparator to the container or to the stream and it orders (and finds the biggest and smallest) by your rule.

For experienced developers: In a TreeSet or TreeMap the comparator also decides what counts as a duplicate, so include enough fields (a tie-breaker) to keep different objects apart.

A comparator as a reusable class

  • Signature: class ByHeight implements Comparator<Fort>
  • Returns: a named comparator
  • Time: O(1) per compare

For freshers: When the same order is used in many places, or has some logic, give it a name: a small class (or a static final constant) that implements Comparator.

For experienced developers: A named comparator can be unit-tested and reused. A static final Comparator<Fort> constant inside the class is a neat middle path.

expert.content:
Rules of a correct comparator

The same contract as compareTo, and the sorting algorithm depends on it.

  • Antisymmetric: sign(compare(a, b)) == -sign(compare(b, a)).
  • Transitive: if a < b and b < c then a < c.
  • A broken comparator can make sort throw IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract, or silently give a wrong order.
  • Avoid subtraction: a.x - b.x overflows. Use Integer.compare.
  • It should be consistent with equals when used in a TreeSet or TreeMap, or two "different" objects will be merged.
  • Sorting objects is stable (TimSort); sorting primitives is not stable but it does not matter there.
Trap: reversed() applies to the whole chain
Trap: a TreeSet comparator that is too loose

Real example: grouping and ranking

Comparators combine with streams to answer "rank the forts" questions in a few lines.

Best practices

Build comparators from small pieces.

  • Prefer Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) over hand-written compare methods.
  • Use comparingInt / Long / Double for primitive fields; never subtract.
  • Add a tie-breaker so the order is total, especially for TreeSet and TreeMap.
  • Use nullsFirst / nullsLast when keys can be null.
  • Keep reusable comparators as static final constants and give them clear names.
  • Remember that reversed() reverses the entire chain built so far.

interviewQA: What is a Comparator?
A functional interface with compare(a, b) that defines an ordering outside the class; it can be passed to sort methods and sorted collections.
Comparable vs Comparator?
Comparable: one natural order inside the class (compareTo). Comparator: any number of external orders (compare), usable on classes you cannot modify.
Is Comparator a functional interface?
Yes (@FunctionalInterface): it has one abstract method, compare, so lambdas and method references work. equals is inherited from Object and does not count.
How do you sort by two fields?
Comparator.comparing(A::x).thenComparing(A::y).
How do you sort in descending order?
Add .reversed() to a comparator, or use Comparator.reverseOrder() for natural order. Be careful that reversed() reverses the whole chain built so far.
How do you sort a list containing nulls?
Wrap with Comparator.nullsFirst(c) or nullsLast(c).
Why use comparingInt instead of comparing?
It avoids boxing each int into an Integer, so it is faster and uses less memory.
What exception can a bad comparator cause?
IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract (from TimSort), or a wrong order without any error.
How does a Comparator affect a TreeSet?
It decides both the order and equality: elements for which compare returns 0 are duplicates and only one is kept.
How do you create a max-heap PriorityQueue?
new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()) or Collections.reverseOrder().
Is sorting a list of objects stable?
Yes, list.sort and Collections.sort use TimSort, which is stable.

topics.name: Internal Working of HashSet

beginner.content:
The big idea: a HashSet is a HashMap

A HashSet does not have its own storage. Inside it holds a HashMap; every element you add becomes a key of that map, and the value is always the same dummy object. So "a Set has no duplicates" is really "a Map has no duplicate keys".

  • Field: private transient HashMap<E, Object> map;
  • Field: private static final Object PRESENT = new Object(); (the shared dummy value)
  • add(e) is map.put(e, PRESENT) == null: it returns true only if the key was new.
  • contains(e) is map.containsKey(e); remove(e) is map.remove(e) == PRESENT.
  • Everything you learnt about HashMap (buckets, collisions, resize, treeification) applies unchanged. See Internal Working of HashMap.

What each HashSet method really calls

intermediate.content:
A HashSet built by hand

Wrapping a HashMap gives you a complete HashSet in a few lines.

MiniHashSet: add, contains, remove

  • Signature: class MiniHashSet<E> { private final HashMap<E, Object> map; }
  • Returns: a working set
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: This is almost exactly the real source of java.util.HashSet. The three core methods are one-line calls to the map; the shared PRESENT object saves memory because no per-element value is created.

For experienced developers: The real class has the same shape. Its constructors only differ in the capacity and load factor they pass to the backing map.

How a duplicate is detected

  • Signature: hash(e) -> bucket -> equals()
  • Returns: true / false
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: When you add an element, the backing map hashes it, goes to the bucket, and compares with every node there: first by hash, then by == or equals. A match means "duplicate": the map keeps the old key and add returns false.

For experienced developers: Note: when a duplicate is rejected, the old object stays in the set; the new one is thrown away. This matters if the two objects are equal but not identical.

Missing hashCode makes duplicates appear

  • Signature: equals() overridden, hashCode() not overridden
  • Returns: a set with duplicates
  • Time: wrong

For freshers: If you override only equals, two "equal" objects usually hash into different buckets, so the set never compares them and keeps both.

For experienced developers: Fix: always override hashCode with the same fields as equals. A record gets both for free.

Constructors and capacity

Each constructor just configures the backing map.

Constructors and the 0.75 / 16 defaults

  • Signature: new HashSet<>(); new HashSet<>(int cap); new HashSet<>(int cap, float load); new HashSet<>(Collection c)
  • Returns: a set
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: new HashSet<>() creates new HashMap<>() (capacity 16, load factor 0.75). The copy constructor sizes the map as max((int)(c.size() / .75f) + 1, 16) so that copying does not trigger a resize.

For experienced developers: Because the backing map has lazy allocation, the array of buckets is created only on the first add.

Ordering and iteration

The order of a HashSet is the order of the backing map's buckets.

Why the order looks random

  • Signature: iteration = map.keySet(): bucket 0 .. n-1
  • Returns: elements in bucket order
  • Time: O(n + capacity)

For freshers: Elements come out in bucket order, which depends on hash codes and the table size, not on the order you added them. After a resize the order can change.

For experienced developers: Never depend on this order. If you need one, use LinkedHashSet (insertion order, whose backing map is a LinkedHashMap) or TreeSet (sorted, backed by a TreeMap).

null in a HashSet and fail-fast iterators

  • Signature: add(null) and for-each + add()
  • Returns: allowed / ConcurrentModificationException
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: A HashSet allows one null element (HashMap allows a null key, stored in bucket 0). Its iterator is fail-fast through the map's modCount: adding or removing during a loop throws ConcurrentModificationException.

For experienced developers: Remove during iteration with iterator.remove() or removeIf.

expert.content:
The real source of java.util.HashSet (simplified)

The implementation is so small that its core fits in this list.

  • public boolean add(E e) { return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null; }
  • public boolean contains(Object o) { return map.containsKey(o); }
  • public boolean remove(Object o) { return map.remove(o) == PRESENT; }
  • public Iterator<E> iterator() { return map.keySet().iterator(); }
  • public int size() { return map.size(); }
  • clone() copies the backing map; serialization writes the elements, capacity and load factor (the map field is transient).
  • A package-private constructor HashSet(int, float, boolean dummy) creates a LinkedHashMap: that is how LinkedHashSet reuses all of HashSet.

Memory: why PRESENT matters

  • Each HashSet element costs one HashMap.Node (about 32 bytes: header, hash, key, value, next) plus its slot in the table. The value field points to the one shared PRESENT object, so it adds nothing.
  • A set of 1 million small objects therefore needs tens of megabytes just for the nodes. If memory is tight and keys are small integers, a BitSet or a primitive-collection library is far smaller.

Mutating an element after adding it

The bucket is chosen when the element is added. If the fields used by hashCode change afterwards, the element sits in the wrong bucket and contains cannot find it any more.

Best practices

Everything about HashSet follows from the HashMap inside it.

  • Elements must implement equals and hashCode consistently (or be records / strings / numbers / enums).
  • Use immutable elements, or never change fields used by hashCode while the object is in a set.
  • Presize a large set: new HashSet<>((int) (n / 0.75f) + 1) (or HashSet.newHashSet(n) in Java 19+).
  • Do not rely on iteration order; choose LinkedHashSet or TreeSet if order matters.
  • For thread safety use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() or Collections.synchronizedSet.

It wraps a HashMap: each element is a key and the value is a shared dummy object PRESENT. add is map.put(e, PRESENT) == null.
How does HashSet avoid duplicates?
The backing HashMap cannot hold duplicate keys: it compares hashCode and then equals; if a match exists put returns the old value and add returns false.
What does HashSet.add() return and why?
true if the element was new (map.put returned null) and false if it already existed.
What is PRESENT?

Why does a HashSet show duplicates when only equals is overridden?

Is HashSet ordered?

Which map backs LinkedHashSet and TreeSet?

Can HashSet contain null?

What happens if you modify an element after adding it?

beginner.content:
The big idea

A HashMap is an array of buckets. To store or find a key, Java turns the key into a number (the hash code), turns that number into an array index, and goes straight to that bucket. That is why get and put take about the same time whether the map holds 10 entries or 10 million.

  • The array is called table; each slot is a bucket holding a chain of Node objects (key, value, hash, next).
  • Default capacity 16 buckets, load factor 0.75: when more than 12 entries exist the table doubles.
  • Two different keys can land in the same bucket: a collision. They share a linked list there.
  • Since Java 8, a long chain (8 or more nodes, with capacity at least 64) becomes a red-black tree.

The four steps of put(key, value)

StepWhat happensCode idea
1. HashCall key.hashCode() and mix the high bits into the low bitsh ^ (h >>> 16)
2. IndexReduce the hash to a bucket number(n - 1) & hash
3. Search the bucketWalk the chain: same hash and equals(key) means "update this node"equals() decides
4. InsertNo match: add a new node at the end of the chain. Resize if size is above the thresholdsize > 0.75 x capacity

Why a power-of-two capacity?

  • When n is a power of two, (n - 1) & hash equals hash % n but is much faster (one AND instruction).
  • It also makes resizing cheap: after doubling, each entry either stays at its index or moves to index + oldCapacity.
  • That is why new HashMap<>(10) actually creates a table of 16: the capacity is rounded up to the next power of two.

intermediate.content:
A HashMap built by hand

The best way to understand it is to write a small one. Each sample below adds one idea.

Node: key, value, hash, next

  • Signature: static class Node { final int hash; final K key; V value; Node next; }
  • Returns: one entry of a bucket chain
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Every entry is a Node. It stores the key, the value, the key's hash (so it need not be recomputed) and a next pointer to the following node in the same bucket.

For experienced developers: In the real java.util.HashMap the class is HashMap.Node; a bucket that turned into a tree holds TreeNode objects instead.

put(): hash, index, search, insert

  • Signature: V put(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the old value or null
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Compute the bucket, walk its chain looking for an equal key. If found, replace the value; otherwise add a node (this miniature adds it at the front of the chain for brevity; the real HashMap appends at the tail). It uses only 4 buckets so you can see collisions.

For experienced developers: The real code first compares hash (cheap int compare) and only then calls equals (possibly expensive). That is why a good hashCode matters.

Collisions and the role of equals() and hashCode()

  • Signature: int hashCode(); boolean equals(Object o)
  • Returns: int / boolean
  • Time: O(1) per call

For freshers: Two keys with the same hash end up in the same chain; equals then tells them apart. The contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes. If you override equals but not hashCode, equal keys land in different buckets and get fails.

For experienced developers: Mutable keys are dangerous: if a field used in hashCode changes after put, the entry sits in the wrong bucket and can never be found again.

Broken hashCode: equal objects in different buckets

  • Signature: class Fort { equals(...) without hashCode(...) }
  • Returns: a map that cannot find its keys
  • Time: O(1) wrong answer

For freshers: This is the most common HashMap bug. Without hashCode, the default (identity-based) hash is used, so two equal forts get different bucket numbers.

For experienced developers: Always override both together, and use the same fields in both. In modern Java a record does it correctly for you.

Resizing

When the table gets too full, it doubles and every entry is re-bucketed.

Load factor, threshold and resize()

  • Signature: threshold = capacity x loadFactor; if (++size > threshold) resize()
  • Returns: a table twice as big
  • Time: O(n) once, O(1) amortised

For freshers: With capacity 16 and load factor 0.75 the threshold is 12. The 13th entry triggers resize(): a new table of 32 buckets, with the threshold now 24.

For experienced developers: Resizing is the most expensive step of a HashMap. If you know the final size, create the map with enough capacity: new HashMap<>((int) (expected / 0.75f) + 1) (or HashMap.newHashMap(expected) in Java 19+).

The resize split: stay or move by oldCapacity

  • Signature: newIndex = oldIndex OR oldIndex + oldCapacity
  • Returns: each entry's new bucket
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: When the capacity doubles from 16 to 32, only one more bit of the hash is used. That bit is 0 (the entry stays) or 1 (it moves exactly oldCapacity places up). Java 8 uses this to split each chain without recomputing.

For experienced developers: The order inside each bucket is preserved by the split, which is also why concurrent resizing no longer makes a cyclic list as in Java 7.

Java 8: chains become trees

Long chains are the only real threat to HashMap speed.

Treeification

  • Signature: TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8; MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64; UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6
  • Returns: a red-black tree bucket
  • Time: O(log n) worst case

For freshers: If a bucket reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the chain becomes a red-black tree, so lookups in that bucket cost O(log n) instead of O(n). With a smaller table, the map resizes instead. When a tree shrinks to 6 or fewer, it turns back into a list.

For experienced developers: Tree nodes are ordered by hash, then by compareTo if the key is Comparable, then by a tie-break. So Comparable keys are friendlier under heavy collisions. It also defends against hash-flooding attacks.

Null key and iteration

Two details that follow from the design.

The null key and iteration order

  • Signature: hash(null) = 0; iteration walks table[0..n-1]
  • Returns: bucket 0 / array order
  • Time: O(n + capacity) to iterate

For freshers: A null key has hash 0, so it always lives in bucket 0. Iteration visits buckets from 0 to n-1 and each chain in order, so the order depends on hashes and capacity, not on insertion order.

For experienced developers: Iterating costs O(size + capacity), so a huge capacity with few entries makes loops slow. The order can change after a resize.

expert.content:
The exact source, in plain words

What java.util.HashMap does for put(key, value) (putVal):

  • hash(key) = key == null ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16).
  • If table is null or empty, resize() creates it (lazy allocation: no array until the first put).
  • Bucket = table[(n - 1) & hash]. If empty, place a new Node there.
  • Otherwise: if the first node matches (hash == and key == or equals) remember it; else if it is a TreeNode use putTreeVal; else walk the chain and, at the end, append a node and call treeifyBin when the chain length reaches 8.
  • If an existing node matched: replace its value (and return the old one); do not change modCount.
  • Else: ++modCount, and if ++size > threshold then resize().
  • New nodes are appended at the tail of the chain in Java 8+ (Java 7 inserted at the head).

Why the hash is spread with h ^ (h >>> 16)

  • The bucket number only uses the low bits of the hash (4 bits for 16 buckets). Many hash codes differ only in their high bits.
  • XOR-ing the top 16 bits into the bottom 16 lets high bits influence the index, spreading keys more evenly at almost no cost.

Fail-fast iterators: modCount

Every structural change (add a new key, remove) increments modCount. An iterator remembers the value it started with and throws ConcurrentModificationException if it differs. Updating the value of an existing key is not structural.
Sizing a HashMap to avoid resizes

HashMap versus ConcurrentHashMap internals

TableNode[] tableNode[] table (volatile reads)
Writing a bucketPlain writeCAS into an empty bucket, otherwise synchronized on the bucket's first node
ReadingPlain readLock-free
Sizeint sizeStriped counters (CounterCell)
ResizeOne threadSeveral threads help migrate buckets
null key / valueAllowedNot allowed
IteratorsFail-fastWeakly consistent (never throw CME)

Best practices

What the internals tell you to do.

  • Override equals and hashCode together, using the same immutable fields (or use a record).
  • Use immutable keys: String, Integer, enums, records.
  • Presize the map when the final size is known.
  • Make keys Comparable if many may collide: the tree bin can use it.
  • Never share a plain HashMap between threads that write; use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Do not rely on iteration order.

interviewQA: How does HashMap work internally?

An array of buckets. put hashes the key, picks the bucket with (n-1) & hash, searches the chain using hash and equals, then updates or appends a node; the table doubles when size exceeds capacity x 0.75.
What is a collision and how is it handled?
Two different keys mapping to the same bucket. They are stored in a linked list in that bucket (a red-black tree when it reaches 8 nodes and the table has 64+ buckets); equals() distinguishes them.
Why must you override hashCode when you override equals?
Equal keys must go to the same bucket; with the default identity hashCode they do not, so get() misses.
What are the default capacity and load factor?
16 and 0.75. The table is allocated lazily on the first put and the threshold is 12.
Why is the capacity always a power of two?
Index = (n - 1) & hash is a fast modulo, and resizing splits each bucket into "stay" and "move by oldCapacity".
What changed in HashMap in Java 8?
Treeification of long chains (O(log n) worst case), tail insertion instead of head insertion, an order-preserving resize split, and no more cyclic-list bug.
It mixes the high 16 bits into the low bits that the index uses, reducing collisions for hashes that differ mostly in high bits.
Where is the null key stored?
Bucket 0, because hash(null) is 0.
What happens if a key is mutated after being put?
Its hash changes, so it is looked up in a different bucket and becomes unreachable: effectively lost.
Is HashMap thread-safe? What happens with concurrent writes?
No. Concurrent writes can lose entries or corrupt the table (Java 7 could loop forever when resizing). Use ConcurrentHashMap.
What is the time complexity of get / put?
O(1) average, O(log n) worst case with treeification (O(n) before Java 8 or for non-comparable colliding keys in a tree bin).
What is modCount?
A counter of structural changes; iterators compare it to the value they saw at creation and throw ConcurrentModificationException if it changed.
